lessons.title: Enums & Match

answers: Nothing — a wildcard arm keeps the match exhaustive
A new variant silently falls into it instead of erroring
It makes the match slower by adding a runtime check
writing.exampleCaption: The `Move` value carries coordinates. A match must cover every variant unless a catch-all deliberately covers the remaining cases.
writing.explanation:
`match` forces every variant to be handled, so adding a new state turns every incomplete match into a compile error instead of a silent bug. Variants can carry data, which lets one type model a whole state machine rather than a bag of loosely related fields.

A boolean can distinguish two states, but it becomes obscure when a feature has several states or each state carries different data. An enum names the alternatives. `Message::Quit` carries nothing, `Message::Move` carries two coordinates, and `Message::Write` carries text. A value is exactly one variant at a time, so code cannot accidentally pair coordinates with a quit message as it might with a loose struct of optional fields.

A `match` examines the variant and binds only the data available in that branch. Every arm must produce a compatible type if the `match` is used as an expression. The compiler's exhaustiveness check is valuable during maintenance: adding `Message::Resize` points to every decision that now needs a policy. A wildcard `_` can be appropriate when all remaining cases truly share the same behavior, but it hides newly added variants if used merely to silence the compiler. For a small state machine, spell out the known cases.

Trace the sample with one value of each variant. Note that `Message::Write(t)` moves its `String` out when the enum is matched by value; match a reference, `match &message`, if you need to keep the original message. Then add a variant with a field and update the rendering match explicitly. This exercise connects data modeling, exhaustive control flow, and ownership. A well-shaped enum makes invalid combinations harder to represent and changes to the model easier to audit.

When the enum is public, adding a variant may require downstream users to update their exhaustive matches. That compile-time interruption is useful: it forces every caller to consider the new state rather than silently treating it as an old one.

An enum is one value chosen from several named variants. A variant can carry data, so `Message::Write(String)` and `Message::Quit` have different shapes under one type. A `match` can handle each shape explicitly. The compiler checks that every possible variant is covered unless you use a wildcard; that guarantee is especially useful when a new variant is added later.

For each variant in the example, write down what data it carries. Then trace a `match`: which arm runs, which fields are bound, and what value the arm produces. Add one new variant and inspect the exhaustiveness error before writing its behavior. Avoid a wildcard when it would hide an important new case. Enums are useful when exactly one state can be active at a time; several independent booleans often allow impossible combinations. Make invalid combinations unrepresentable where the domain rules are stable.
writing.feedback: A catch-all removes the compiler's help exactly when you add a state.
writing.question: What does the wildcard cost you?
writing.rule: `match` is exhaustive: every variant must be handled.
writing.success: The local compiler accepts the changed solution and the separate verification harness finishes all normal and boundary cases. Printing a success message alone does not complete this lab.
writing.summary: Enums model a value that is exactly one of several variants.

lessons.title: Option & Result

answers: Result<T, E>
Option<T>
A panic
writing.exampleCaption: `?` returns early on the error case, keeping the happy path flat.
writing.explanation:
Pattern matching and the `?` operator keep both cases explicit without null, sentinel values, or exceptions. Reach for `Option` when absence is normal and expected, and `Result` when the caller needs to know why something did not work.

Ask what the caller needs to know when there is no value. If a search simply finds nothing, `Option<T>` describes the two normal outcomes: `Some(item)` or `None`. If a parser fails, `Result<T, E>` describes success plus a reason for failure. Neither type is a disguised boolean. They carry the successful value, and `Result` preserves information needed to explain or recover from the error.

Use `match` when both outcomes deserve visible behavior. `if let Some(item) = lookup()` is compact when you only care about the present case. `map` transforms a value inside `Some` or `Ok` without inventing a value for the other case. `unwrap_or` supplies a deliberate default; use it only when the default is genuinely correct. `?` can return early for an absent `Option` or an error `Result` when the surrounding function has the appropriate return type. A function returning `Result` cannot use `?` on an `Option` without explicitly choosing what error absence means.

For the exercise, make `find(id)` return `Option<Item>` because missing data is expected. Make `parse_id(raw)` return `Result<u32, ParseIntError>` because malformed input has a reason. Combine them in a caller: parse first, then look up, and show distinct messages for malformed and unknown IDs. Avoid `unwrap()` on both paths; it collapses two normal situations into a panic. Good types help the caller write a useful interface.

`Option<T>` answers whether a value is present. `Some(T)` carries the value; `None` means absence. `Result<T, E>` answers whether an operation succeeded. `Ok(T)` carries success; `Err(E)` carries a reason for failure. They are different questions. A search that finds no item may return `None`; a failed file read needs an error that explains what went wrong. Choosing the right type tells callers what decision to make.

Take a lookup function and test three cases: item found, item missing, and storage unavailable. If the last case is possible, a single `Option` cannot communicate it well; consider `Result<Option<T>, E>`. Unwrap only when you have proved the variant or intentionally want to crash on an invariant violation. Prefer `match`, `if let`, or combinators when they keep both paths visible. Ask what information a caller needs at the boundary, then choose the return type.
writing.feedback: There is no error to report — absence is the expected outcome.
writing.question: Which return type fits 'the item may simply not exist'?
writing.rule: `Option` for absence, `Result` when the caller needs the reason.

writing.summary: `Option` models absence; `Result` models failure with a reason.

lessons.title: Collections

answers: It avoids hashing the key at all
It looks the key up once instead of twice
It keeps the map sorted by insertion order
writing.exampleCaption: The complete program counts three tokens into two keys, then sorts rows for stable output: crab 1, rust 2.
writing.explanation:
Choosing a collection is part of the model, not an afterthought: order, uniqueness, and key access all change what your code can promise. Each of these owns its data, so passing one around follows exactly the same ownership rules as any other value.

Choose a collection by the operations the program promises. `Vec<T>` preserves an ordered sequence and supports indexed access; appending is a natural operation. `HashMap<K, V>` associates keys with values and is useful for lookup or counting, but its iteration order is not a stable presentation order. A `String` owns UTF-8 text rather than an arbitrary sequence of characters. Naming the data structure early keeps later code from relying on an accidental property, such as hash iteration looking sorted in one run.

The `entry` API handles the common "insert if missing, then update" operation in one lookup. `counts.entry(word).or_insert(0)` returns a mutable reference to the existing count or to a newly inserted zero. Dereferencing it lets the code increment the stored value. Separate `get` and `insert` operations can repeat lookup work. Some nested method-call forms compile under modern Rust borrowing rules; do not assume they always cause a borrow error. The useful distinction is that `entry` directly expresses one keyed slot and returns mutable access to its stored value. Read the type of the returned reference to see why `*count += 1` is needed.

For practice, count words in a short sentence with one repeated word. Print the count for a known key and use `get` to handle an unknown key safely. Then sort the keys before displaying all counts if predictable output matters. Consider ownership as well: keys borrowed from a longer-lived input can be `&str`; keys assembled while parsing may need owned `String` values. The collection's shape, lookup behavior, and ownership together define the data model.

Pick a collection from the operations you need. `Vec<T>` keeps an ordered, growable sequence and is good for iteration and indexing. `HashMap<K, V>` associates keys with values and supports expected fast lookup, with hashing and memory overhead. `String` owns UTF-8 text and can grow. They all own their elements or bytes, so borrowing an element is different from removing or moving it.

Start with a list of names. If you need to preserve their order and print every name, use a vector. If you need to find one name by a unique ID repeatedly, consider a map. Add a duplicate key to a map and observe whether insertion replaces an earlier value. Then inspect the return type of `get`: it may be absent, and a returned reference remains tied to the collection. Choose the data structure after writing down required operations, expected input size, and whether order matters.
writing.feedback: `entry` looks the key up once, exposes the occupied or vacant slot, and returns mutable access to its value. It still hashes the key, and it does not sort the map.
writing.question: Why is `entry()` better here?
writing.rule: `entry().or_insert()` gives you a mutable reference either way.

answers: word.len()
word.chars().count()
word.bytes().len()
writing.exampleCaption: `café` has five UTF-8 bytes and four scalars; the decomposed accented letter has three bytes and two scalars.
writing.explanation:
`String` owns a growable UTF-8 buffer and `&str` borrows one. Rust strings do not support integer indexing such as `s[0]`. Choose `.bytes()` for encoded bytes, `.chars()` for Unicode scalar values, or `.get(range)` for a fallible byte slice. A direct invalid byte-range slice can still panic, so rejecting integer indexing does not eliminate every encoding-related mistake.

UTF-8 stores text as bytes, and a visible character may require more than one byte. In `café`, `len()` is five bytes, while `chars().count()` yields four Unicode scalar values. Neither number necessarily counts what a person sees as a grapheme: a letter plus a combining accent can be two scalar values displayed as one. Rust deliberately makes the unit explicit, so you cannot assume that the fifth byte begins a character.

A `String` owns and can grow its buffer. A `&str` borrows a valid slice of UTF-8 text, whether the source is a string literal or part of a `String`. Slicing by byte ranges is allowed only at character boundaries; a range ending in the middle of a multibyte character fails. Use `.chars()` for scalar-value iteration, `.bytes()` for protocol or encoding work, and `.char_indices()` when you need both a character and its starting byte offset. Avoid repeatedly using `.chars().nth(n)` as if it were constant-time indexing: it walks from the start each time.

Try printing the bytes, characters, and byte offsets of `café` and `naïve`. Predict which offsets jump by more than one. If your UI needs user-perceived character counts or cursor movement, use a Unicode grapheme library and state that requirement explicitly. For many programs, the safest first step is to ask whether the problem is about bytes, scalar values, or displayed clusters before choosing an operation.

If you must slice text, use a checked operation such as `get(range)` when a range may come from external input. It returns `Option<&str>` instead of panicking at an invalid UTF-8 boundary.

`String` owns growable UTF-8 bytes; `&str` borrows a view of UTF-8 text. A string literal has type `&'static str`, but a function accepting `&str` can also receive a borrowed view of a `String`. This is why read-only parameters commonly use `&str`: callers need not give away ownership. Appending to a `String` may reallocate its storage, so a reference into it cannot remain live while a mutation would invalidate that reference.

Try passing both a string literal and a borrowed `String` to the same read-only function. Then change the function to take `String` and observe the move at the call site. Use `.as_str()` or `&value` when you need a view. For slicing, remember that offsets are UTF-8 byte positions and must fall on valid character boundaries. If your task is to count or split what a human sees as characters, specify whether you mean bytes, Unicode scalar values, or grapheme clusters before writing the algorithm.
writing.feedback: `chars().count()` decodes Unicode scalar values. `len()` and `bytes().len()` count bytes; neither is a general visible-character count.
writing.question: Which expression counts Unicode scalar values in `word`?
writing.rule: `len()` counts UTF-8 bytes; `chars().count()` counts Unicode scalar values, not grapheme clusters.

writing.summary: Rust strings are UTF-8, so there is no cheap index by character.

lessons.title: Pattern Matching

answers: It replaces the pattern that precedes it
Adds a condition the arm must also satisfy
It makes the match non-exhaustive on its own
writing.exampleCaption: One arm can test, bind, and destructure at the same time.
writing.explanation:
Patterns work in `match`, `if let`, `while let`, function parameters, and plain `let`. Guards add a condition, `@` binds a value while testing it, and `|` matches several shapes at once. The compiler checks exhaustiveness, so a pattern set that misses a case is an error rather than a surprise at runtime.

A pattern describes the shape of a value and may bind its parts. In the tuple example, `(0, 0)` recognizes one exact point, `(x, 0) | (0, x)` recognizes either axis, and `(x, y) if y < 0` adds a guard. Arms run top to bottom: the first matching arm wins. That order matters because a broad arm placed early can make a later, more specific arm unreachable. Read a `match` as a decision table, then test one input per row and one input at a boundary.

Patterns also appear outside `match`. `let (width, height) = size;` destructures a tuple directly when the shape always fits. `if let Some(value) = maybe_value` handles a single interesting enum case and lets the rest continue. `while let Some(item) = stack.pop()` repeats until the pattern no longer fits. Use a full `match` when every case deserves an explicit policy or when you want the compiler to point out a newly added variant.

A guard is checked after the pattern binds names. It narrows an arm, but it does not generally count as covering every possible value of that shape. In the practice example, an even `Some(n)` goes to the guarded arm, an odd one to the next `Some(n)` arm, and `None` to its own arm. Remove the second `Some` arm and observe the exhaustiveness error. That exercise shows why patterns are more than compact syntax: they make the cases you have and have not considered visible.

Use a small table of example inputs when a pattern has alternatives and guards. That makes overlap visible: an axis point that also satisfies a negative-coordinate guard reaches the earlier axis arm. Reorder only when the intended priority is clear.

A pattern describes the shape of a value while optionally giving names to its parts. In `match`, each arm pairs a pattern with behavior. Matching an enum makes its active variant explicit; matching a tuple can bind two positions at once. A wildcard `_` discards a value you do not need. Use it deliberately, because it can also hide a newly added enum variant that deserves handling.

Read one pattern aloud: 'If this is `Some(value)`, bind the contained value and run this arm.' Then trace the alternative `None` arm. Add a guard only when the variant alone is insufficient, and check whether another arm still covers the remaining values. Try destructuring a struct with two fields and rename one local binding to avoid confusion with the field name. Patterns are a way to state what must be true before a branch runs; the compiler checks the coverage while you decide the behavior.
writing.feedback: A guard is an extra condition; exhaustiveness is still checked across the arms.
writing.question: What does the `if n % 2 == 0` part do?
writing.rule: A guard narrows an arm; the compiler still demands the set be exhaustive.
writing.success: The local compiler accepts the changed solution and the separate verification harness finishes all normal and boundary cases. Printing a success message alone does not complete this lab.

lessons.title: Derive Macros

answers: A struct cannot derive Debug when it has fields
NoDebug does not implement Debug, so the field cannot be printed
Debug always has to be written by hand for structs
writing.exampleCaption: Four traits, no hand-written code, all checked by the compiler.
writing.explanation:
`#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]` generates the mechanical implementation for each field. It only works when every field also implements the trait, which turns a missing capability deep in a struct into a clear compile error naming the field.

A trait describes a capability. `Debug` supports development formatting with `{:?}`; `Clone` makes an explicit copy; `PartialEq` enables equality comparisons; `Default` provides a conventional initial value. `#[derive(...)]` asks the compiler to generate straightforward implementations for a struct or enum. The generated code follows the fields: if a field cannot be cloned or printed, the containing type cannot derive that capability automatically.

Derive only the traits a type needs. Cloning a large structure can be expensive and may hide a design that should borrow instead. A default value is useful when it is meaningful, but `Config::default()` is a poor substitute for required settings that must be supplied by the caller. For an enum, deriving `Default` needs one designated default variant. Generated `PartialEq` compares corresponding fields, which might be wrong for a domain concept whose identity is based only on an ID. In that case, write the behavior deliberately rather than assuming the mechanical result is right.

Try the sample with `println!("{a:?}")`, `a == b`, and `a.clone()`. Then add a field whose type lacks `Debug` and inspect the compiler error; derive or implement `Debug` for that field if printing it is appropriate. This shows how trait bounds propagate through a model. Treat a derive list as part of the public promises of a type, and keep those promises intentional.

A derived `Debug` formatter can reveal sensitive fields. Before printing a configuration or token-bearing struct in diagnostics, decide whether to implement a redacted formatter instead. Compiler-generated convenience still deserves a review of what it exposes.

A derive asks the compiler to generate an implementation of a trait for a type. `#[derive(Debug)]` enables debug formatting, and common derives such as `Clone`, `Copy`, `PartialEq`, and `Eq` carry different contracts. Deriving is possible only when the type's fields support the requested trait. It does not make every operation free: cloning an owned `String` allocates, while copying a small integer is cheap.

For the example type, predict whether two values can be compared, printed with `{:?}`, or copied after assignment. Add one derive at a time and inspect any error about an unsupported field. Then add `Copy` to the derive list and see why the `String` in `host` rules it out. Do not derive traits merely to silence an error. Ask what callers should be allowed to do and what cost or semantics that operation has. A generated implementation is still part of your public type's behavior.
writing.feedback: A derived `impl` is only as available as the traits of its fields.
writing.question: Why can that struct not be printed?
writing.rule: `derive` only compiles when every field also implements the trait.
writing.success: The struct prints with `{:?}` and compares with `==` without manual code.
writing.summary: `derive` writes the obvious implementation so you do not have to.
writing.task: Derive the traits a small struct needs to be printed and compared.

Before reading code, name the smallest piece of information that must survive from one step to the next. A scan turns a sequence into a small piece of state. The core mechanism is this: Visit every element once and stop when the predicate is satisfied. Treat it as a claim to test after every operation. Write down the state before the first operation, update it once, and ask which part of the claim is still true. If an item is skipped, inserted, or removed, explain why that action cannot destroy an answer that should be retained. lessons.title: Ownership

answers: Add mut to a
Use a.clone() for b
Wrap a in a Box
writing.exampleCaption: The move is what makes a double free impossible.
writing.explanation:
Moves transfer that responsibility to a new binding and make the old one unusable. Copy types duplicate instead of moving, and Drop runs the moment the owner leaves scope — which is how Rust frees memory with no garbage collector and no possibility of a double free. When you genuinely need two usable values, `clone()` makes a second one that owns its own data.

Think of ownership as the answer to one question: who is responsible for cleaning up this value? A `String` owns a growable heap buffer, so there must be a single owner when that buffer is released. In the example, `first` initially owns it. `let second = first` transfers that responsibility; it does not make a second buffer. If both bindings could free the same allocation, the program would be unsound, so the compiler refuses to use `first` afterward.

Trace the example line by line. Before the assignment, `first` is valid. After it, only `second` is valid. At the end of the scope, `second` is dropped and its buffer is freed once. For a small integer, assignment behaves differently because `i32` implements `Copy`: both bindings contain independent bits and remain usable. When you need two independent strings, `.clone()` creates another allocation, and the explicit call shows the cost.

Ownership is also an API design tool. A function taking `String` may keep or transform the value; one taking `&str` only needs to read it. Before adding a clone to silence a move error, ask whether the function should borrow instead. Try passing the example string to a printing function first by value and then by reference. Observe which signature lets the caller print it again. The compiler error identifies where the value moved; use that location to decide who should own the data next.

The same move rule applies when a value enters a collection or is returned from a function. Follow the owner rather than memorizing special cases for each syntax form.
writing.feedback: Cloning creates a second owned `String` rather than moving the first.
writing.question: What is the smallest fix that keeps both usable?
writing.rule: One value, one owner; a move ends the previous binding.
writing.success: You can explain why no double free is possible.
writing.summary: Ownership gives every value one clear cleanup responsibility.

lessons.title: Borrowing

answers: Make items immutable
Move the println! above the push
Clone the whole vector
writing.exampleCaption: The borrow ends at its last use, and the push is fine after that.
writing.explanation:
Rust permits many shared references or exactly one mutable reference, never both. The compiler tracks the region where each borrow is actually used, so a borrow ends at its last use rather than at the end of the block — which is why moving one line is often the whole fix.

Borrowing lets a function use data while its owner remains responsible for it. A shared reference, written `&T`, permits reading; many readers can coexist. A mutable reference, `&mut T`, permits writing but must have exclusive access for the duration of that borrow. This rule prevents a reader from holding a pointer into a vector while a writer grows the vector and possibly moves its buffer.

In the example, `first` points at the first element of `items`. The print is its last use. Only after that point does `items.push(...)` change the vector. Reverse those two lines and the shared borrow overlaps the mutation; the compiler rejects the code. The lexical braces are not the only clue: modern borrow checking follows the actual last use. This is why rearranging an operation can solve the conflict without adding a clone or another container.

For practice, first read two elements through separate shared references; both are allowed. Then try to push while either reference is still used later. Read the error as a timeline: identify when the read borrow starts, its final use, and where the write was attempted. Move the write after those uses or finish the reads first. Avoid treating every borrow error as a reason to copy data. Most are signals that the program needs a clearer order of operations. When the order truly cannot change, reconsider the structure that owns the data.

A shared borrow does not promise that the underlying allocation is immortal. It only prevents incompatible mutation while the reference is used. That distinction matters whenever a container might resize or be dropped.
writing.feedback: Ending the shared borrow before the mutation is the minimal change.
writing.question: What is the smallest edit that fixes it?
writing.rule: Many shared borrows or one mutable borrow, never both at once.
writing.success: Check passes, Run prints `crab`, and the `Vec` is still extended.
writing.summary: Borrowing lets code use a value without taking ownership.

lessons.title: Slices

answers: A newly allocated String the caller owns
A borrowed view tied to the input's lifetime
A copy of the first three bytes of the input
writing.exampleCaption: No allocation, and the result cannot outlive its input.
writing.explanation:
A slice stores a pointer and a length but owns nothing, so creating one allocates no memory. Because it borrows, the compiler will not let it outlive the `String` or array it points into, which rules out a dangling view.

A slice is a view into existing contiguous data. `&str` views UTF-8 text, while `&[T]` views elements such as integers in an array or vector. A slice carries a starting address and a length; it does not allocate a new buffer or become a second owner. That makes slice parameters useful for read-only APIs: a function accepting `&str` can read both a string literal and a portion of an owned `String`.

The `first_word` example finds a byte offset for a space, then returns either the prefix or the whole input. The returned `&str` refers to the caller's data. The function cannot safely return a slice of a local `String` created inside it, because that local owner would be dropped on return. The borrow checker ties the view's validity to the source data. The same reasoning applies to `&items[1..3]`: changing the vector's storage while the slice remains in use would invalidate the view.

Try calling `first_word` with "crab rust" and with "crab". Check both results, then pass a substring of a larger string. To make an independent copy, call `.to_owned()` or `.to_string()` deliberately and compare the ownership behavior. For Unicode text, slice indices are byte offsets and must fall on UTF-8 boundaries; arbitrary numeric character positions are not safe byte positions. Decide whether an API needs a borrowed view or an owned copy based on how long the result must survive.
writing.feedback: The returned `&str` borrows from text, so it cannot outlive it.
writing.question: What does that return type mean?
writing.rule: A slice borrows a range; it allocates nothing.

lessons.title: Copy & Clone

answers: Add mut to name
Use name.clone() for alias
Wrap it in a Box
writing.exampleCaption: The integer copies; the `String` would have moved without `.clone()`.
writing.explanation:
Types whose fields are all `Copy` and which do not implement `Drop` can implement `Copy`, so assigning them leaves the original usable. An owning `String` or `Vec` is not `Copy`; duplicating those owners requires an explicit operation such as `.clone()` — the cost is visible in the source rather than hidden in an assignment.

`Copy` means a value can be duplicated by copying its bits, with no visible method call. Primitive integers and many small plain-data structs qualify. A type with a destructor cannot be `Copy`, because two implicit copies would both try to perform cleanup. `String` owns a heap allocation and therefore moves on ordinary assignment. `Clone` is different: it is an explicit operation, and its cost depends on the type. Cloning a `String` duplicates its bytes into a new buffer.

In the sample, `a` and `b` are separate integers after `let b = a`, so both print. The string expression uses `s.clone()` to create `t`; after that, both own their own text. If you change the line to `let t = s`, only `t` remains usable. The output may look identical when you do clone, but the memory and performance behavior are not. That is why Rust makes the expensive path visible.

Do not add `.clone()` automatically whenever the compiler reports a move. Ask whether the next operation only needs `&T`, whether ownership can be transferred to the right place, or whether two independent values are genuinely required. Try deriving `Copy` for a struct containing only `u32` fields, then add a `String` field and read the new error. This reveals the trait requirement through a concrete type. Use cloning when independent ownership is part of the design, and borrowing when the other code only needs temporary access.

An `Arc<T>` clone illustrates another nuance: it usually increments a reference count rather than duplicating all the data inside. The method name means an explicit duplicate of the value’s ownership handle, not necessarily a deep copy of every reachable byte.

`Copy` is a semantic contract, not a promise that the value is small or cheap: a large array of Copy elements is still Copy. `Clone` need not deep-copy data; cloning an `Arc<T>` shares the same allocation and increments its reference count. Decide whether the API needs another owner or independent data.
writing.feedback: Cloning creates a second owned `String`, so the original binding stays valid.
writing.question: How do you make that compile without changing the println?
writing.rule: `Copy` permits implicit bitwise duplication; `Clone` is explicit and has a type-specific cost.

lessons.title: Drop & Scope

answers: dropping a
after explicit drop
dropping b
writing.exampleCaption: At each scope end, the last declared remaining local drops first.
writing.explanation:
When a value goes out of scope its Drop implementation runs, and remaining local bindings in a scope drop in reverse declaration order. This is deterministic — no collector decides later — which is what lets Rust manage files, locks, and sockets with the same mechanism it uses for memory.

Rust cleans up owned resources at predictable points. When a scope ends, its local values are dropped in reverse declaration order; nested scopes finish before their outer scope continues. `Drop` is a trait whose `drop` method runs during that cleanup. It can release a file, unlock a mutex guard, or close a connection. Memory is only one resource governed by the same rule.

Follow the `Noisy` example and predict the messages before running it. The inner value is created after the outer values and disappears at the inner closing brace. At the outer closing brace, the remaining locals drop from last declared to first declared. The printed order is evidence of the ownership timeline. Binding a value with a leading underscore still owns it; the underscore only suppresses an unused-variable warning. If you need to release a value earlier, `std::mem::drop(value)` consumes it explicitly.

A destructor should not be where essential business logic hides, because callers cannot see that work from the return type. It should reliably release or finalize a resource. Also remember that moving a value transfers the eventual drop to its new owner; the old binding does not run a second destructor. Try moving one `Noisy` value into a helper function and record where its message appears. The exercise connects scope, movement, and cleanup without relying on a garbage collector or manual free call.

When several fields belong to one struct, their cleanup order follows the struct’s field declaration order after the struct’s own Drop method runs. Keep resource dependencies in mind if one field’s destructor relies on another resource.
writing.feedback: `a` is dropped early by hand; `b` still drops at the end of the scope.
writing.question: Which of those messages prints last?
writing.rule: At scope end, remaining locals drop in reverse declaration order; struct fields drop in declaration order.
writing.success: You can explain why `dropping a` prints before `after explicit drop`, and `dropping b` after it.
writing.summary: Cleanup runs at a place you can point to in the source.

answers: Two inputs mean the compiler cannot tell which one the result borrows from
A &str return always needs an annotation

writing.exampleCaption: One name ties the result to both inputs.
writing.explanation:
An annotation does not change how long anything lives. It tells the compiler how input and output borrows are connected, so it can prove a returned reference never outlives the data behind it. Most of the time inference handles this and you write nothing at all.

A lifetime is a relationship the compiler uses to prove a reference is valid when it is used. It is not a timer and an annotation cannot keep memory alive. In `longest`, both input references are related to the returned reference through `'a`. The caller must use the result only while the selected input could still be valid. This is conservative: at compile time the function could return either argument, so the result is limited by the shorter applicable borrow.

Trace a call where one string lives for the whole function and another is created in an inner block. You may compare them and print the chosen slice inside that block. You cannot keep the returned reference for use after the inner string has gone away, because it might point into that string. Moving a lifetime annotation to a different letter would not change the data's scope. The remedy is to shorten the use of the result, return an owned `String`, or change which data the result can borrow from.

Most functions do not need written lifetime parameters. A function with one borrowed input and a borrowed output often has an obvious relationship, and Rust applies elision rules. Add annotations when multiple inputs make the source of the output ambiguous or when a struct stores a reference. In an error message, identify the owner of each referenced value and the last point at which it is alive. That timeline is more useful than trying random apostrophe labels until the code compiles.

writing.exampleCaption: The bound names only what the body actually needs.
writing.explanation:
Trait bounds state exactly the capabilities the generic body needs, and the compiler generates a specialised copy per concrete type. This can avoid trait-object dispatch and enable inlining, but it does not make the body, allocations or copies free. Specialization can increase code size and compile time; a bound wider than necessary also narrows who can call you.

Generics let one implementation describe several concrete types without erasing what those types are. In the `largest` example, `T` is a placeholder chosen by the caller. The function does not need to know how to print or clone `T`; it only compares references, so `PartialOrd` is the capability that matters. A bound is a promise to the compiler about which operations the body may use, and it is a constraint on every caller. Adding `Clone` because it seems convenient would exclude useful types for no reason.

Read the signature from outside in: the input is a borrowed slice of `T`, and the output is a borrowed `T` from that slice. The function does not allocate or return a new owned value. It starts with the first item, walks the rest, and updates the best reference. This also reveals a precondition: indexing `items[0]` panics for an empty slice. A production API should state that precondition or return `Option<&T>` so emptiness is handled explicitly. Generic code still needs careful edge-case design.

At compilation, calls with concrete types can be specialized, so no runtime type switch is needed for a normal generic function. Try the function with integers and then with a comparable custom type. Make an empty input test and redesign the return type if that case should be safe. Finally, ask whether the chosen bound expresses precisely the behavior used. The aim is reusable code with an honest contract, not the longest possible list of trait bounds.

lessons.title: Traits

answers: Vec<impl Shape>
Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>
Vec<S: Shape>
writing.exampleCaption: The same trait, reached two different ways.
writing.explanation:
A concrete generic instantiation normally selects the implementation statically and may allow inlining. `dyn Trait` defers the choice to runtime through a vtable, which permits heterogeneous values behind pointers. The actual cost depends on the workload and optimizer; dynamic dispatch does not itself require a heap allocation. A dyn value has no size the compiler can plan for, so it lives behind a pointer: `Box<dyn Trait>` is what goes into a `Vec`.

A trait names behavior that multiple types can provide. `Shape::area` describes what a caller may ask without assuming how a circle or rectangle stores its dimensions. A generic parameter `S: Shape` selects a concrete implementation at compile time; a `&dyn Shape` or `Box<dyn Shape>` selects through a trait object at runtime. Both use the same trait contract, but they solve different API problems.

Use generics when a function can operate on one concrete type per call and compile-time specialization is useful. Use a trait object when a collection must hold values of several concrete types together or when a choice is only known at runtime. Because concrete types can have different sizes, `dyn Shape` is unsized and needs a pointer such as `&dyn Shape` or `Box<dyn Shape>`. The pointer includes enough information to reach the value and its method table. That indirection has a cost, but it can simplify an extensible design.

Try implementing `Shape` for two structs, then call both `a(&shape)` and `b(&shape)` from the example. Put both shapes into a vector of boxed trait objects and sum their areas. Notice the tradeoff: you can call methods exposed by `Shape`, but concrete-only methods are not directly available through the trait object. Write the shared contract at the level callers need, and prefer the simpler generic form unless mixed runtime values are a real requirement.

A trait is most useful when it describes a coherent capability, not simply several methods that happen to be near each other. Keep implementations predictable so generic callers can rely on the contract. When a method needs the concrete `Self` type or a generic parameter, check whether that method should be unavailable through `dyn Trait` or placed in a separate trait.
writing.feedback: A trait object erases the concrete type so the elements share one size.
writing.question: What replaces `???` so one `Vec` can hold both shapes?
writing.rule: Use generics for static dispatch and trait objects for dynamic dispatch; neither choice alone determines performance.

writing.explanation:
Elision handles the common shapes, so you write annotations only when the relationship is genuinely ambiguous — typically when several references go in and one comes out. A struct holding a reference needs one too, because the struct cannot outlive what it borrows.

A reference field makes a struct dependent on data owned elsewhere. `Excerpt<'a>` says its `part` cannot be used after the borrowed text becomes invalid. Move the use inside the block, or change the struct to own its data. Neither fix requires an invented longer lifetime label.

Lifetime elision saves annotations in signatures with an obvious input-output relationship. Explicit names become useful when a returned reference could come from several inputs, or when a type stores references. A name such as `'a` means the linked borrows must satisfy the same validity relationship; it does not mean they were created at the same time or live for exactly the same duration. lessons.title: Closures

answers: Fn
FnMut
FnOnce
writing.exampleCaption: Two closures: `read` only reads `total`, and `bump` mutates `count`.
writing.explanation:
Rust infers whether a closure needs a shared borrow (`Fn`), a mutable borrow (`FnMut`), or ownership (`FnOnce`) from what the body does. `move` forces capture by value, but sending a closure to another thread also requires `Send` and suitable lifetimes. Moving a reference does not extend the referent’s lifetime, and moving an `Rc` does not make it `Send`.

A closure is a callable value that may carry data from the surrounding scope. The first example only reads `total`, so it can satisfy `Fn`; the second changes `count`, so it needs mutable access and satisfies `FnMut`. A closure that consumes a captured value may be callable only once and satisfy `FnOnce`. These traits describe what callers may do with the closure, not just what the closure returns.

Capture is inferred per variable. A shared read usually borrows, a mutation needs an exclusive borrow, and consuming an owned value may move it into the closure. The `move` keyword forces capture by value, but it does not automatically make every call consume the captured value. A moved-in `String` can still be read on repeated calls if the body only borrows it. This distinction matters for thread work: unscoped `thread::spawn` requires a `Send + 'static` closure. Owned captures are one way to satisfy the lifetime bound; references to static data can also work. Scoped threads may borrow local data because they are joined before the scope exits.

Run the sample and try to read `count` while the mutating closure will be called again. The active mutable borrow explains the compiler's objection. Call the closure for the last time before reading the value, or confine it to a shorter scope. Then write a closure that calls `drop(name)` to see why it becomes `FnOnce`. Choose a callback bound based on how often the caller must invoke it and whether mutation is part of the contract.

A closure can capture different variables in different ways. One captured counter may be mutated while another captured configuration is only read. Reason about each capture separately instead of assigning one ownership mode to the whole surrounding scope.

All closures implement `FnOnce`. A closure that can be called through mutable access also implements `FnMut`; one callable through shared access also implements `Fn`. These bounds form a hierarchy, not three disjoint categories. Interior mutability can change data through a shared reference without requiring an `FnMut` receiver.

writing.exampleCaption: Nothing runs until collect asks for items.
writing.explanation:
map and filter build a description of the work; nothing runs until a consumer such as collect, sum, or a for loop asks for items. That laziness is why a long chain still makes a single pass over the data instead of one pass per step.

An iterator is a sequence of values produced on demand. Calling `.filter()` or `.map()` builds another iterator; it does not run the closure over every element immediately. A consumer such as `.collect()`, `.sum()`, or a `for` loop pulls values through the chain. In the example, each requested output asks the filter for the next even input, then squares that value. There is no separate vector of filtered values unless you explicitly collect one.

This laziness can save allocations and allow early stopping. Add `.take(2)` before collecting and only two matching results are needed. Conversely, if you want to reuse results repeatedly, collecting may be the right choice. Be attentive to item types: `.iter()` yields references, `.iter_mut()` yields mutable references, and `.into_iter()` consumes the collection. A chain that looks visually similar can therefore borrow, mutate, or move its source.

For practice, insert a temporary `inspect` adapter that prints each value passing a stage. Observe that nothing prints before the consumer runs. Then change the consumer from `collect` to `sum` and predict the answer. Finally, try to use the original collection after `.into_iter()` and after `.iter()`. `Iterator` syntax is most readable when the operations tell a clear story—selection, transformation, then consumption—and when ownership of the source is intentional.

A lazy chain is useful only when a consumer eventually requests values. If you create an iterator and discard it, even a `map` closure with a print statement will never run. Use a loop for side effects when that intent is clearer.

writing.rule: Adapters are lazy; a consumer is what makes the work happen.

writing.exampleCaption: Only `next` is written; `take` and `sum` come for free.
writing.explanation:
`Iterator` requires only next(); everything else — map, filter, take, zip, sum — arrives as default methods. That is why a custom sequence composes with the standard library exactly like `vec.iter()` does, without any of it knowing your type exists.

Implementing `Iterator` means defining the type of each item and one method, `next`. Each call either returns `Some(item)` and advances internal state or returns `None` when the sequence is finished. The default adapters then work automatically because they are expressed in terms of repeated `next` calls. That is the core composability advantage: your `Fibonacci` can be filtered, zipped, limited, and summed like an iterator from the standard library.

Walk through the sample with initial `a` and `b` values. Record the returned `value` before updating the state, then compute the pair for the next call. Test the first six outputs by hand. For an unbounded sequence, a consumer like `collect::<Vec<_>>()` would never finish; use `.take(n)` or another finite stopping rule. Also consider arithmetic overflow: with `u64`, sufficiently large Fibonacci numbers exceed the type. Decide whether `next` should stop with `None`, use checked addition, or deliberately wrap, and document that choice.

A good custom iterator keeps `next` small and makes its state invariant clear. If the sequence owns its data, consuming it may be natural; if callers need the source afterward, return an iterator that borrows it. Implement `size_hint` only when you can provide a truthful bound. The small required interface is powerful, but correctness of state transitions remains your responsibility.

`None` normally means the sequence has ended. Consumers may ask for `next()` again, so document whether your iterator stays finished; implementing `FusedIterator` is an additional promise only when that behavior is guaranteed. Test the terminal state and any overflow boundary, not merely the first few values.

A final call after completion should have a documented outcome.

lessons.title: Associated Types

answers: Never, associated types are always better
When one type should implement the trait several times
Only for iterators
writing.exampleCaption: One implementation per type, so the output never has to be annotated.
writing.explanation:
A trait parameter can distinguish multiple implementations for the same implementing type. An associated type is chosen by each particular implementation; a trait may have both parameters and associated types. For a non-generic trait such as `Iterator`, one implementation fixes that type’s `Item`. `Iterator` uses `Item` this way, which is why you write `Iterator<Item = u32>` rather than passing the element type at every call site.

An associated type is a type chosen by a particular implementation of a trait. `Iterator::Item` is the classic example: once a type implements `Iterator`, its `Item` is fixed for that implementation. A caller can write a bound such as `I: Iterator<Item = u32>` to say exactly which stream it accepts. This is different from giving the trait a type parameter that might allow the same implementer to implement several versions.

In the `Container` example, `Bag` chooses `String` for `Item`. The `get` method then returns `Option<&String>`, borrowing an element from the bag rather than copying it. Read `Option<&Self::Item>` from the inside out: there may be no element, and when there is one, it is a reference to the implementer's chosen item type. Try changing the bag to hold `u32`; the associated type declaration and implementation return type must change together.

Associated types make caller signatures shorter and communicate that there is one natural output type for a given implementation. They do not make a value dynamic at runtime. Compare a trait with `type Item` to a generic trait parameter in a toy design and ask whether a single implementer should reasonably have multiple item types. Choose the form that matches the relationship in your model. The compiler will enforce the choice wherever the trait is used.

An associated type also helps documentation: the implementation can name its element once, and every method uses that same choice. This is useful for parsers, streams, and containers where one implementer has a natural output. If an API really needs several output types for the same implementer, a generic trait parameter may describe the contract better.
writing.feedback: `From<T>` is generic precisely because a type converts from many others.
writing.question: When should you prefer a generic parameter instead?
writing.rule: An associated type is fixed per trait implementation; trait parameters can distinguish implementations for the same type.
writing.success: `parse` returns that type, and callers never have to name it.
writing.summary: An associated type fixes one output type per implementation.
writing.task: Implement `Parser` once by choosing its `Output` type.

answers: Into is derived alongside From automatically

writing.exampleCaption: `Add` powers `+` and `Display` powers `{}`, so `Money` reads like a built-in.
writing.explanation:
`a + b` calls `Add::add`, `{}` calls `Display::fmt`, and `.into()` calls `Into`, which you get for free by implementing `From`. Because they are normal traits, your own types participate in the same syntax as the built-in ones, and the compiler checks the result type at every use.

Operator syntax in Rust is backed by trait implementations. `a + b` invokes `Add::add`, and the implementation selects an associated `Output` type. In the `Money` example, adding two money values yields another `Money`; the newtype prevents an ordinary integer from being treated as money without an explicit conversion. This is useful because a small wrapper can make invalid operations harder to write while keeping familiar arithmetic syntax.

Do not overload an operator merely because you can. Readers expect `+` to combine values predictably; surprising side effects or hidden I/O make code harder to trust. Decide whether addition consumes operands, borrows them, or needs multiple implementations. The sample's `Money` is `Copy`, so by-value addition is cheap. A large owned type may benefit from reference-based implementations to avoid unnecessary moves. Use checked arithmetic or a wider representation if overflow matters for the domain.

`Display` and `Debug` serve different readers: `Display` is an intentional user-facing representation, while `Debug` helps inspect a value during development. `From<T> for U` expresses an infallible conversion and provides `Into<U>` automatically; a fallible conversion belongs in `TryFrom`. Implement a formatter for `Money`, add two values, and compare the result with your expected units. Keep the trait's semantic promise as clear as its syntax.

For a domain type, specify units and error behavior before implementing arithmetic. Money measured in cents should not add to a temperature, and a conversion from floating-point input may be lossy or fallible. A `From` implementation must not hide a failure; use `TryFrom` when invalid input is possible. Write tests for zero, negative values if allowed, and overflow boundaries. Operator syntax makes code compact, but the type system and tests must keep its meaning precise.
writing.feedback: The standard library has `impl<T, U: From<T>> Into<U> for T`.
writing.question: Why does `.into()` work without writing an `Into` impl?
writing.rule: Implement From, and Into is generated for you — never implement both.
writing.success: `500_u32.into()` produces a `Money`, and you can say where its `Into` came from.
writing.summary: Operators and conversions are ordinary traits you can implement.

answers: String is Copy
inspect only borrowed it
println! restores it
writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
A parameter of type `String` takes ownership, while `&str` only borrows text. Read the signature before deciding whether the caller should keep using its value.

A function signature is an ownership map. `fn inspect(text: &str)` asks for temporary read access and lets the caller keep its `String`. `fn store(text: String)` takes ownership, so the caller cannot use that binding after the call unless the function returns it or the caller cloned it beforehand. A parameter like `i32` is passed by value too, but `i32` is `Copy`, which leaves the original usable. The syntax is the same; the type determines the effect.

Walk through the example: `name` owns its bytes, `&name` creates a borrowed view for `inspect`, and the borrow ends after its final use in the call. The last `println!` can therefore read `name`. Change `inspect` to accept `String` and pass `name` without `&`; the final print now triggers a move error. Returning a `String` is a legitimate design if the function transforms ownership, but a printing helper has no reason to consume its input.

When designing an API, use `&str` if any UTF-8 text view will do, `&String` only when the `String` container itself matters, and `String` when ownership or mutation independent of the caller is required. For mutable access without transfer, use `&mut String`. Try calling one borrowed helper with both a string literal and an owned string. The more flexible signature often makes the surrounding code simpler and avoids clones inserted only to satisfy an unnecessarily consuming function.
writing.feedback: Correct: inspect only borrowed it.
writing.question: Why can name be printed after inspect?
writing.rule: A parameter of type `String` takes ownership, while `&str` only borrows text.
writing.success: You can say why `name` stays usable, and what would change if `inspect` took `String`.

lessons.title: Mutable Borrows

answers: Shared read access
Exclusive write access

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
An `&mut` reference permits mutation without transferring ownership. Exclusivity lasts through its final use, preventing another reader or writer from observing a half-finished update.

An `&mut T` gives one caller exclusive temporary access to a value. The owner still exists, but it cannot read or write through another path while the mutable borrow is active. This is more than a rule about syntax: it prevents a reader from seeing a partially updated structure and prevents two writers from racing to change the same state. After the last use of the borrow, the owner can be used again.

In `add_one`, the star in `*value += 1` follows the mutable reference to the integer it points at. `score` must be declared `mut` so it can be borrowed mutably. The call lends access; it does not move `score` into the function. The final print shows the updated owned value. Try storing `let edit = &mut score;`, then attempt to print `score` before `edit` is last used. The compiler flags the overlapping access. Move the print after that last use and the program becomes valid.

The same pattern applies to methods on vectors and structs. A mutable borrow lets a helper change an object in place without returning a replacement object. Keep the exclusive region short and meaningful. If a large function needs many unrelated mutable borrows, split it into operations with clear boundaries. This can make borrow errors easier to diagnose and can reveal which fields should be separate. Reach for interior mutability only when ordinary exclusive borrowing cannot express the actual access pattern.
writing.feedback: Correct: Exclusive write access.
writing.question: What does `&mut` grant temporarily?
writing.rule: An `&mut` reference permits mutation without transferring ownership.
writing.success: You can say why `score` can be read again on the last line, and what it holds.
writing.summary: One temporary writer with exclusive access.

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
Passing `&mut *value` creates a shorter reborrow instead of moving the original mutable reference. This lets a helper work briefly and returns control to the outer borrower afterward.

A mutable reference can temporarily lend its access to another function. In `twice`, each `bump(&mut *value)` creates a shorter reborrow from the outer `&mut i32`. The first helper finishes before the second begins. The original reference is not consumed, so it can be used again after the helper calls. The important property is the timeline: there is one active writer at a time.

The `*` dereferences the outer reference to the value, and `&mut` forms a new mutable borrow of it. Rust often performs this reborrow implicitly at a call site, but writing it out makes the mechanism visible. If the first helper kept the reference beyond its call, the second exclusive borrow could not start. A return value tied to that borrow may also keep it active. Read compiler errors as a sequence of active loans rather than as a demand to clone a mutable reference; mutable references are not freely duplicable.

Try adding a print through `value` between the two `bump` calls, then after both calls. Both are fine if each reborrow has ended. Next, return the first reborrow from a helper and try to call `bump` again before its last use; the conflict shows why the short duration matters. Reborrowing is common in methods that coordinate several mutating helpers, and understanding it keeps such code simple without resorting to shared runtime mutation.

level borrowed it

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
Destructuring can move an owned field and copy or borrow the rest. After a partial move the whole struct is unavailable, but fields that were not moved may still be used directly.

A struct can be partly moved when one field owns data and another field is still independently usable. In the example, `user.name` is a `String`, so assigning it to `name` transfers that field's ownership. `user.level` is a `u8`, so it can still be read and copied. The whole `user` value can no longer be used as a complete `User` because one of its fields is missing. The compiler tracks that state precisely.

This is useful when consuming one payload but retaining metadata. Destructure a value and decide for each field whether to move, copy, or borrow it. A pattern such as `let User { name, ref level } = user;` moves `name` and borrows `level`. If you need the original struct intact, borrow the name instead of moving it, or clone only that field when an independent owned copy is truly needed. Cloning the entire struct is often wasteful and hides the intended ownership transfer.

Try printing `name` and `user.level`, then attempt `println!("{user:?}")` after the move and inspect the error. Rebuild a new `User` from the moved name and copied level to see how ownership can be reassembled. Types implementing `Drop` cannot have individual fields moved out this way, because their destructor expects a complete value. In those cases, consider replacing a field through an `Option` or using an API that consumes the whole object deliberately.

With larger structs, destructuring at the boundary of a function can make the intended field-level ownership transfer clearer than scattered accesses throughout the body.

lessons.title: Interior Mutability

answers: At runtime
In Cargo.lock
It does not check
writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
`Cell` and `RefCell` allow mutation behind an immutable outer binding. `RefCell` enforces the same shared-or-exclusive rule at runtime and panics if code violates it.

Normal Rust borrowing checks shared readers and exclusive writers at compile time. `RefCell<T>` moves that particular check to runtime for single-threaded code. An immutable binding can contain a `RefCell<Vec<_>>`, and calling `borrow_mut()` can still modify the vector inside. The outer reference is immutable; the cell enforces the inner access rule with a runtime borrow counter. It does not turn conflicting access into something safe to ignore.

In the sample, the temporary mutable guard from `borrow_mut()` ends after `push`, so a later `borrow()` is allowed. Keep a `RefMut` guard in a variable and try calling `borrow()` before dropping that guard: the program panics because a writer and reader would overlap. The fallible `try_borrow()` and `try_borrow_mut()` variants return an error instead of panicking, which can be useful when a conflict is a normal possibility. Hold guards for as short a period as practical.

`RefCell<T>` is not the tool for sharing mutable data across threads; types such as `Mutex<T>` address synchronization there. Use interior mutability when the surrounding API legitimately needs a shared outer reference while an inner value changes, such as a test spy or a local cache. Do not use it to escape a confusing borrow error before understanding the original ownership model. Runtime checks trade earlier compiler feedback for a more flexible access pattern, so that trade should be intentional.

lessons.title: Lifetime Elision

answers: Every &str already has a static lifetime
One input determines output

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
Rust omits obvious lifetime annotations using a small set of rules. One borrowed input can usually determine the returned borrow, keeping signatures readable without weakening the proof.

Elision means the compiler fills in common lifetime relationships you did not write. In `fn first(text: &str) -> &str`, the only borrowed input is `text`, so the returned slice must be tied to it. The function cannot create a reference that outlives the caller's text. Writing the equivalent named lifetime can be educational, but it does not make the result live longer or change runtime behavior.

The simple rules become less obvious with two borrowed inputs. A function `fn choose(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str` leaves the compiler unable to know which input the result borrows from. If the body can return either, name a shared relationship in the signature. If the result always comes from `a`, make that explicit. Methods have a useful convention: when `&self` is an input, an elided output borrow is tied to `self` unless you specify otherwise. These are rules of signature interpretation, not guesses based on the function body.

Practice by writing the explicit version of `first` and checking that it compiles exactly as before. Then add a second borrowed parameter used only as a search needle; if the return still comes from `text`, annotate that relationship accurately. Draw arrows from the output reference back to the input that owns its data. This skill makes API signatures easier to read and avoids over-annotating code where elision already communicates the contract clearly.

lessons.title: Owned or Borrowed?

answers: It creates new text
&str is slower

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
Return a borrow when the result is a view into an input; return an owned value when new data is created or must escape independently. The choice affects allocation and API flexibility.

The lifetime of the data behind a return value should determine its type. `trimmed(input: &str) -> &str` returns a view into existing bytes, so it can avoid allocation, but the caller cannot keep the result after the input is gone. `label(input: &str) -> String` creates uppercase text in a new owned buffer. The caller may keep that buffer independently of the input. Neither choice is universally better; each promises a different relationship.

Follow the example with a `String` created in an inner block. A borrowed trimmed view must be used before the source leaves the block. An owned uppercase result can be moved out and printed afterward. If a function sometimes borrows and sometimes must allocate, `std::borrow::Cow<'a, str>` can express either case, but it adds complexity that a beginner API may not need. First choose a clear owned or borrowed contract, then optimize if measurements justify it.

Do not return a reference to a local `String` assembled inside a function; the value would be dropped when the function returns. Return that `String` by value instead, relying on move semantics. Conversely, do not allocate just to return a substring that the caller will use briefly while the input remains alive. Test both signatures with a string literal and with an owned string. Ask who owns the bytes after the call and how long the result must remain valid; those answers should make the return type feel inevitable.

A borrowed return can still be ergonomic: callers can call `.to_owned()` only when they need independence. That lets the common short-lived path avoid allocation while preserving an explicit escape hatch.
writing.feedback: Correct: It creates new text.
writing.question: Why does label return `String`?
writing.rule: Return a borrow when the result is a view into an input; return an owned value when new data is created or must escape independently.
writing.success: You can say which result can outlive `input`, and why each return type fits its body.
writing.summary: Choose a return type that matches the data flow.

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
A trait object stores a pointer to data and a table of methods. It enables mixed concrete types in one collection at the cost of dynamic dispatch and some optimization opportunities.

A trait object lets code work with a value whose concrete type is chosen at runtime. `Box<dyn Draw>` owns a value on the heap while exposing only the `Draw` behavior. A vector of these boxes can contain buttons, charts, and labels as long as each implements `Draw`. A generic `Vec<T>` normally has one concrete `T` for all entries, so it cannot directly hold several unrelated structs. The trait object is the bridge when a heterogeneous collection is genuinely needed.

At a call to `item.draw()`, the program follows a method table associated with that value's concrete type. This adds an indirection and can limit some optimizations, but it also means new implementers can join the collection without rewriting the renderer. The object still obeys ownership rules: the vector owns the boxes, and borrowing the slice for `render` does not consume them. `&dyn Draw` would borrow a single drawable instead of owning it.

The trait must be usable as an object; not every trait method fits. A method that returns bare `Self` or is generic over another type may need a `where Self: Sized` restriction or a different design. Start with a small behavior contract such as `draw(&self)`. Implement it for two types, store both in one vector, and count the calls. Use static generic dispatch when all values have one concrete type known at compile time. Choose dynamic dispatch for the runtime mixture, not as a default for every trait.

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
A generic `impl` can grant a trait to all types satisfying a bound. Blanket implementations are powerful because they shape which future implementations remain legal under coherence rules.

A blanket implementation defines one rule for every type satisfying a bound. In the example, any sized `T` that implements `Display` also receives `Named`, whose `name()` delegates to `to_string()`. This avoids writing essentially the same implementation for each printable type. The benefit is broad, but so is the commitment: every current and future `Display` type covered by the rule gets that behavior.

Trace a call on an integer and one on a custom struct with `Display`. Both resolve to the same generic implementation, specialized for their concrete type. A type without `Display` has no `Named` implementation from this blanket rule, so a caller demanding `Named` cannot use it. The implicit `Sized` bound on `T` also leaves out `str` itself, unless the `impl` adds `?Sized`. This is a compile-time capability relationship, not a runtime registry. The code does not inspect the type's name or perform a dynamic check.

Blanket implementations interact with coherence. If your crate already grants `Named` to all `Display` types, a more specific `Named` implementation for one overlapping `Display` type conflicts on stable Rust. Also, the orphan rules limit which trait/type combinations your crate may implement. Before publishing a broad blanket `impl`, ask whether future special cases should behave differently. Try adding an overlapping implementation and read the compiler error. Sometimes a newtype wrapper or a narrower bound gives users more room to customize behavior later.

As a design exercise, imagine a type whose `Display` format changes over time. Would the generated name remain appropriate? A blanket rule is strongest when the mapping from the bound to the new behavior is stable for all covered types.

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
A trait may provide a method body that implementations inherit. Defaults reduce repetition, while required methods still define the minimum contract each type must supply.

A default method supplies behavior that implementers may inherit. In `Summary`, each type must provide `title()`, while `summary()` can be built from that required method. A new type gets a useful summary immediately after implementing the minimal contract. It may override the default when its presentation needs more context, but callers can still rely on the trait method existing.

This is a way to centralize a policy that is genuinely shared. If the default silently makes assumptions that are false for some types, it can produce misleading output. Keep required methods small and explicit, and make the default's dependency on them visible. For example, `summary()` calls `self.title()` so the implementation's title is always reflected. If the trait grows a new required method, every implementer must update; if it grows a default method, existing implementers usually continue to compile.

Create two structs implementing `Summary`: one inherits `summary()`, and the other overrides it. Call both through a generic function constrained by `Summary` and compare output. Then imagine a third type with no meaningful title. That is a sign the trait may be the wrong abstraction for that type, even if a placeholder string would make it compile. Good defaults reduce repetition while preserving an honest contract for every implementation.

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
A function may be generic over both a data type and a lifetime. Keep each parameter only when the body needs it; extra bounds make an API less reusable without adding safety.

The `choose` signature has two independent kinds of abstraction. `T: PartialOrd` says what operation the body may perform on the values: comparison. `'a` says how long the borrowed inputs and returned reference are related. These parameters solve different problems. Replacing the lifetime with a broader trait bound cannot make a dangling reference safe, and adding a lifetime cannot make an incomparable type satisfy `PartialOrd`.

The result borrows one of the two inputs. Because the body may choose either, the caller must use it only while both candidate sources are valid. Suppose the left value lives throughout a function and the right value lives in an inner block. Calling `choose` and using the result inside the block is fine. Keeping the result for use after that block is not, because it might point to the right value. The generic type does not change this rule; it applies whether `T` is an integer, a string wrapper, or a custom ordered type.

Try calling `choose` with two `i32` values, then with a custom type that implements `PartialOrd`. Next, create one input in a smaller scope and observe the lifetime error when the result escapes it. Fix the use site, not the annotation label. Keep trait bounds as narrow as the implementation needs, and keep lifetime relationships as specific as the returned data requires. A clear signature explains both the operation and the ownership story.

The letter chosen for a lifetime has no special power. Rename it consistently and the contract is the same. The useful information is which references share the label and which output is tied to them.

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
Adapters such as map and filter describe work but do nothing until a consumer asks for values. A clear pipeline separates selection, transformation, and collection without temporary vectors.

An iterator pipeline can read like a data-processing sentence: choose items, transform each chosen item, then consume the result. The sample starts with borrowed values from an array, filters for even numbers, squares them, and sums the squares. The final answer is 20 for `[1, 2, 3, 4]`. The adapters are lazy; `sum()` repeatedly pulls the next item through the chain. No intermediate vector is required.

Look closely at references. `values.iter()` yields `&i32`, while `filter` passes a reference to each item into its predicate, so the closure sees an extra reference layer and the example uses `**v`. The following `map` receives each item as a plain `&i32`, and `v * v` needs no star because multiplication is also implemented for references. Writing types beside the closures for one exercise can demystify those stars. If you use `into_iter()` on an owned vector instead, values are moved into the pipeline, changing what remains available afterward.

Use `inspect` temporarily to see when each element reaches a stage. Then insert `.take(1)` before `sum()` and predict which elements are evaluated. lessons.title: Closure Capture Modes

answers: Capture ownership
Return type
Call syntax
writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
A closure borrows, mutably borrows, or moves each captured value according to its body. The move keyword transfers captures even when the body would otherwise only borrow them.

The callable traits describe how a closure uses its captured environment. A closure that only reads captures can be called through `Fn`. One that mutates a captured variable needs `FnMut`, so the closure value must be mutable when invoked. One that consumes a captured value may be callable only once and satisfies `FnOnce`. `Fn` is the most reusable capability; `FnOnce` is the least demanding bound for a caller that invokes a callback exactly once.

In the sample, `move` transfers `name` into `announce`, allowing the closure to own the string independently of the original binding. But the body merely prints by borrowing its captured string, so the closure can still be called more than once. Add `drop(name)` inside the body and it consumes the capture; a second call then fails. This is why `move` and `FnOnce` should not be treated as synonyms. Capturing by value answers who owns the data; the body determines what kind of calls remain possible.

Experiment with three closures: read a counter, increment it, and consume a string. Try passing each to functions bounded by `Fn`, `FnMut`, and `FnOnce`, then read the errors. A callback API should ask for no more capability than it needs. If it calls the callback once, an `FnOnce` bound accepts the widest set of closures. If it may call repeatedly without mutable access to the closure, `Fn` is the right promise.

writing.rule: A closure borrows, mutably borrows, or moves each captured value according to its body.

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
PhantomData tells the type system that a zero-sized marker matters to ownership or state. It enables APIs where illegal transitions have no callable method, without adding runtime storage.

`PhantomData<T>` is a zero-sized marker that tells the compiler a type is logically related to `T` even when it stores no `T` value. In `Job<State>`, the state appears only at the type level. `Job<Ready>` and `Job<Running>` can have the same runtime fields but expose different methods. A transition can consume one state and return another, so calling a `finish` method on a job that was never started becomes a compile-time error.

`PhantomData<T>` itself has guaranteed size zero and alignment one for every `T`. The containing structure still follows its own layout rules. The marker has no runtime payload, but it is not decorative. It affects how the compiler reasons about ownership, variance, drop checking, and automatic traits in more advanced code. That is why the choice of marker type matters in low-level APIs. In a beginner typestate design, the central idea is simpler: the state is represented by a type rather than a boolean field that every method must check at runtime.

Sketch a `start(self) -> Job<Running>` method defined only for `Job<Ready>`, then a `finish(self) -> Job<Done>` defined only for `Job<Running>`. Try calling `finish` on the original ready job and inspect the method-not-found error. Notice that each transition consumes its old state, preventing two parallel versions of the same logical job from being used accidentally. Use this pattern when invalid transitions are costly enough to justify the extra types; a small ordinary enum may be clearer for a simple runtime choice.
writing.feedback: `PhantomData<T>` is guaranteed to have size 0 and alignment 1 for every `T`. Its ownership, variance and auto-trait effects still matter; the containing structure has its own layout.
writing.question: What layout is guaranteed for `PhantomData<T>` itself?
