lessons.title: Send & Sync

answers: RefCell is not Sync, and its runtime check is not atomic
A closure is not allowed to capture a cell type
borrow_mut needs an unsafe block to compile
writing.exampleCaption: The bound is what the thread API asks for, spelled out.
writing.explanation:
`Send` means a value can be moved to another thread; `Sync` means `&T` can be shared with one. Both are inferred from a type's fields, so you rarely write them — but they are why `Rc` is rejected at compile time while `Arc` is accepted, and why a whole class of race is a type error.

`Send` and `Sync` are marker traits describing safe movement and sharing across threads. A `Send` value may transfer ownership to another thread. A `Sync` type may be accessed through shared references from multiple threads; equivalently, `&T` can be `Send` when `T` is `Sync`. These properties are usually derived automatically from fields, so the type composition communicates the safety constraint.

`Rc<T>` changes a non-atomic reference count, so it is unsuitable for sharing between threads. `Arc<T>` uses an atomic count, but that does not make arbitrary inner mutation safe. If workers must change the contained value, combine it with a suitable synchronization primitive such as `Mutex<T>`, or use atomics for a very narrow operation. The compiler rejecting `Rc` in a spawned thread is evidence of a missing thread-safety guarantee, not an invitation to add `unsafe impl` casually.

Test this by capturing an `Rc<String>` in a thread closure and reading the diagnostic. Replace it with `Arc<String>` for read-only sharing. Then try to mutate a shared counter and choose `Arc<Mutex<i32>>` or `Arc<AtomicUsize>` based on the operation. Ask separately whether ownership crosses threads and whether references may be shared. `Send` and `Sync` answer those two different questions; they do not promise freedom from deadlocks, starvation, or application-level ordering mistakes.

A value can be `Send` without being `Sync`, so moving it exclusively to another thread may work even when simultaneous shared references would not. Check the precise compiler bound at the thread or library boundary. This tells you whether to change ownership, add synchronization, or redesign the data flow. Never assert these marker traits manually unless you can prove the `unsafe` contract for every field and operation.

writing.rule: `T` is `Sync` exactly when `&T` is `Send`.
writing.success: You can explain the difference in terms of the count, not the API.
writing.summary: Two auto traits decide what may cross a thread boundary.
writing.task: Name why one shared pointer crosses threads and the other does not.

answers: working, printed as soon as the future is built
Nothing — the future is never awaited
It panics because nothing ever polls it
writing.exampleCaption: Nothing happens until the future is awaited or spawned.
writing.explanation:
Calling an `async fn` does nothing on its own: it builds a state machine that makes progress only when polled. `.await` yields at that point, letting the executor run something else while the operation is pending — which is how one thread can service thousands of waits.

Calling an `async fn` creates a future that represents work to be performed. It does not run the body to completion immediately. An executor polls the future; it may return `Poll::Pending`, register a way to be woken, and yield the thread to other tasks. When the awaited operation can make progress, the waker schedules another poll. Eventually the future returns `Poll::Ready(value)`. This is why many I/O waits can share a small number of threads.

An `.await` marks a point where the task may suspend. Local values that are needed afterward become part of the future's state, which affects memory usage and whether the future can be safely sent between executor threads. Code between `await` points still runs synchronously until it yields or completes, so a long CPU loop can monopolize an executor worker even though it sits inside an `async` function.

Write a short `async` function that logs before and after an awaited timer. Observe that constructing its future does not print the whole sequence; running it on an executor does. Then launch two timer futures concurrently and compare the elapsed time with running them one after the other. Avoid thinking of each future as a thread. A future is a state machine plus a polling contract; the runtime decides when and where to poll it. That distinction helps you choose between `async` waiting, blocking work, and true parallel computation.

A future normally needs to be polled by an executor to make progress. Merely storing it in a variable does not schedule it. That is a common source of confusion when an `async` call appears to do nothing. Trace where the future is awaited, spawned, or otherwise polled.
writing.feedback: The future is created and dropped without ever being polled.
writing.question: What does that print with no `await`?
writing.rule: Futures are lazy: no poll, no progress.
writing.success: You can say why the body has not executed at that point.
writing.summary: An `async` function returns a future that has not run yet.
writing.task: Explain what a call to an `async fn` actually produces.

answers: main is not allowed to print before awaiting
main cannot be async without a runtime to poll it
async fn is still unstable in this edition
writing.exampleCaption: A synchronous main explicitly asks a current-thread executor to poll the future.
writing.explanation:
The language defines `Future` and `.await`; polling, timers, and I/O readiness come from a runtime you choose, such as tokio or smol. That keeps `async` usable on an embedded target with no allocator, at the cost of one decision you have to make per project.

Rust's language and standard library define `Future` and `.await`, but a program needs an executor to poll futures and often a runtime to provide timers, sockets, and task spawning. Tokio is a common choice, but an `async` function is not inherently tied to one runtime. A library should be clear about whether it uses runtime-specific I/O types or exposes runtime-neutral futures. The decision affects how easily callers can integrate it.

The runtime schedules ready tasks; it cannot make blocking code magically nonblocking. A synchronous file operation or long CPU loop inside an `async` task can occupy an executor worker and delay unrelated tasks. Use the runtime's dedicated blocking facility for genuinely blocking work, and measure when offloading is worthwhile. Also know who owns spawned tasks: dropping a join handle does not necessarily cancel the task, depending on the runtime API. Cancellation and shutdown behavior belong in the program's design.

Create a minimal program with an `async` entry point and an awaited timer. Then remove the runtime wrapper and inspect the compiler or execution setup needed to drive the future. Add a second task and observe that scheduling depends on `await` points. When choosing a runtime for a project, check required I/O, platform support, footprint, and shutdown semantics. For embedded or restricted targets, the executor can be much smaller than a server runtime, but you still need a concrete way to poll and wake futures.

An executor and an operating-system event source solve different problems: one chooses which ready future to poll, while the other reports that I/O is ready. A runtime often bundles both. This separation explains why creating a future is cheap but actually driving a network request requires runtime services.

Local Cargo profile: open the supplied project in Crabrix or the browser Playground. Explicitly prepare its pinned Cargo packages once on each device, then Run and Debug compile and execute on that device without a backend. The project includes Cargo.lock. The lesson question remains the completion exercise; running an unchanged demonstration does not prove a separate programming challenge. Tokio 1.54.1 is built with default-features=false and only rt/sync. The current-thread builder needs no runtime attribute macro. JoinSet, Semaphore, watch and yield_now are real Tokio APIs. This profile supplies cooperative concurrency, not native threads, sockets, OS signals or CPU parallelism.
writing.feedback: Something has to drive the future, and that something is the runtime.
writing.question: Why is that not a valid program entry point?
writing.rule: std defines `Future`; the executor is a library decision.
writing.success: You can name polling, waking, and I/O readiness as runtime concerns.
writing.summary: Rust ships the `async` syntax but not the engine that drives it.

writing.exampleCaption: join overlaps the waits instead of adding them up.
writing.explanation:
join runs futures at the same time and waits for all of them; select takes whichever finishes first. Dropping an owned operation future stops polling that operation, but completed external effects remain. A handle to independently spawned work is different: dropping a Tokio `JoinHandle` detaches the task rather than stopping it.

`join!` polls several futures concurrently and waits for all of them; it does not imply they run on separate threads. `select!` waits for one branch to become ready and then proceeds with that branch. The other in-progress branch futures may be dropped when the selection expression ends, depending on how they are owned. Dropping the actual operation future prevents its later polls; cleanup of owned values runs, but ordinary code after its suspension point does not. External effects already performed are not automatically rolled back.

In the example, loading a user and loading orders are independent, so `join!` can overlap their waits. If one result is enough, `select!` might reduce latency, but the losing operation must be safe to stop or resume. A database write followed by an acknowledgement is a dangerous candidate if cancellation can occur between them. Place durable state changes and retries behind an idempotent operation or an explicit transaction where appropriate.

Try timing two independent sleeps with sequential awaits and then with `join!`. Predict the total duration. Next, use `select!` between a timer and a slow operation, and record which cleanup code runs when the slow future loses. Do not assume `async` cancellation works like killing an OS thread; it occurs when an owned future is dropped, usually at a suspension boundary. Choose the combinator from the result you need and the cancellation guarantees of each branch.

When using a timeout wrapper, inspect whether it owns the inner future or only borrows it. That determines whether the timed-out operation is dropped or can continue elsewhere. In either case, record which effects are safe to repeat. If independent operations can fail separately, also decide whether `join!` should wait for every outcome or stop early through a different combinator.

Task ownership matters in timeouts: `timeout(limit, operation())` owns the operation, while timing out a spawned task’s owned `JoinHandle` can merely drop the handle and leave the task running. To request cancellation of an async Tokio task, retain the handle, call `abort()`, and await it to observe termination. Cancellation is cooperative and cannot interrupt a poll that never yields; an already running `spawn_blocking` closure cannot be stopped this way. Use a shutdown protocol for work with effects that must finish or roll back explicitly.
writing.feedback: Sequential awaits serialise work that could have overlapped.

let b = load_orders().await;
writing.question: What is wrong with that if the two are independent?
writing.rule: Dropping an owned operation future stops polling it; dropping Tokio’s `JoinHandle` detaches its spawned task.
writing.success: Total time is the slower of the two, not their sum.
writing.summary: Concurrency inside one task comes from combinators, not threads.

spawn copies the whole array
writing.exampleCaption: Every scoped thread finishes before `scope` returns, so borrowing `values` is allowed.
writing.explanation:
`thread::scope` proves every spawned thread finishes before borrowed stack data disappears. It avoids unnecessary `Arc` or cloning when concurrency stays inside one lexical operation.

Ordinary `thread::spawn` may outlive the function that created it, so its closure generally needs owned, thread-safe data. `thread::scope` sets a tighter boundary: every scoped thread finishes before the scope returns. Within that boundary, a worker can borrow local values that remain alive until all workers join. This is useful for parallel processing of disjoint parts of a collection without cloning the entire collection into `Arc`.

The safety promise is about lifetime, not completion without failure. A scoped worker can still panic; the scope joins all its workers and can propagate an unhandled panic. Write the error policy explicitly if a worker result matters. Also avoid making the borrow invalid yourself: if one worker reads a value, the usual borrowing rules still prevent an overlapping mutable borrow of that same value. A scope is no shortcut around aliasing or synchronization.

Try dividing a slice into two non-overlapping mutable halves with `split_at_mut`, then process one half in each scoped worker. Predict why the compiler accepts those two borrows. Change the code so both workers try to mutate the entire slice and read the rejection. Finally compare the scoped form with an owned `Vec` moved into an ordinary spawned thread. Use the scope when the work naturally ends inside the current operation; use detached or longer-lived tasks only when you have an explicit ownership and shutdown plan.
writing.feedback: `thread::scope` joins every thread before it returns, so a borrow of `values` cannot outlive the array. `split_at_mut` keeps the two mutable borrows disjoint.
writing.question: Why may these threads borrow from values?
writing.rule: `thread::scope` proves every spawned thread finishes before borrowed stack data disappears.
writing.success: You can say why two disjoint `&mut` halves compile and why two mutable borrows of `values` do not.

The lock is slow

writing.exampleCaption: `lock` returns `Err` after a holder panicked, and `into_inner` still gives access to the guard.
writing.explanation:
A standard `Mutex` becomes poisoned when a holder panics. Recovery is possible, but code must decide whether the protected invariant is still trustworthy instead of blindly ignoring the signal.

A standard-library `Mutex` becomes poisoned if a thread panics while holding its guard. A subsequent `lock()` returns a `PoisonError` rather than silently claiming the protected state is sound. The bytes are still there, and the error can give access to the guard, but the application must decide whether its invariant survived. Poisoning is a warning about a possible inconsistency, not proof that the data is corrupt.

Imagine a bank ledger with two fields updated under one lock. If a panic occurs after subtracting from one field but before adding to the other, a future reader must not pretend the transfer completed. Recover only after checking or rebuilding the invariant. A cache whose entries are independently replaceable might be safe to clear and rebuild. A process-wide critical invariant may justify failing the operation instead. The right choice comes from the meaning of the state, not from a universal `unwrap()` habit.

Write a test in which a worker acquires a mutex and deliberately panics. Join that worker, then inspect the result of the next `lock()`. Separate the panic returned by `join()` from the poison returned by `lock()`: they are two observable events. Add a recovery branch that validates the stored data before clearing poison or continuing. Avoid putting fallible, unrelated work inside a critical section so the chance of leaving a half-updated invariant is smaller. Different mutex implementations have different poison semantics, so verify the actual API you use.
writing.feedback: `lock` returns `Err` because a thread panicked while holding the guard. The value is still there, but its invariant may be incomplete.
writing.question: What does poisoning report?
writing.rule: A standard `Mutex` becomes poisoned when a holder panics.
writing.success: You can separate the panic returned by `join` from the poison returned by `lock`, and say when recovery is justified.

writing.explanation:
Atomic operations are indivisible but still need an ordering that describes cross-thread visibility. Use the weakest ordering justified by a written synchronization argument, not by habit.

An atomic value supports operations that are indivisible with respect to competing threads. `fetch_add` on `AtomicUsize`, for example, prevents two workers from losing an increment by reading and writing the same stale count. This makes atomics a good fit for simple counters, flags, and some carefully designed state machines. It does not turn a sequence of several atomic operations into one transaction. If two fields must change together, a mutex may express the invariant more clearly.

Memory ordering answers a second question: when another thread sees an atomic change, which ordinary memory writes are guaranteed visible too? `Relaxed` is enough for a count whose only requirement is an accurate final total after workers join. A flag that publishes prepared data generally needs a release store and an acquire load, or another synchronization design. `SeqCst` gives a stronger global ordering model, but choosing it blindly does not fix a flawed state machine.

lessons.title: Deadlock Avoidance

answers: Both workers lock in one order

writing.exampleCaption: Sorting by id gives every transfer the same first lock, so two transfers cannot wait on each other.
writing.explanation:
Rust prevents data races, not deadlocks. A consistent order for acquiring multiple locks and avoiding calls into unknown code while locked remove common wait cycles.

A deadlock can arise when worker A holds lock X while waiting for Y and worker B holds Y while waiting for X. Both workers may be perfectly data-race-free, yet neither can move. Rust's ownership rules do not decide a global lock order for your program. The simplest prevention is often a consistent acquisition order: if every path takes X before Y, the cycle cannot form from those two locks.

Draw a wait-for graph with one node per task and an arrow when it waits for a resource held by another task. A cycle is the warning sign. Reduce the number of locks held at once, move expensive work outside locked sections, or combine related fields under a single mutex when the data model allows it. `try_lock` can avoid indefinite waiting in some designs, but a retry loop without backoff can livelock or waste CPU. Timeouts help detection and recovery; they do not automatically make a transfer atomic.

Ask what happens if a callback called while holding X attempts to acquire X again: a non-reentrant mutex may self-deadlock. Avoid invoking unknown callbacks while a guard is alive. When reviewing a codebase, document the lock hierarchy near the shared state, not only in one caller. Tests can expose some schedules; a clear acquisition rule is the stronger argument that a cycle cannot occur.
writing.feedback: Both workers take `X` before `Y`, so neither can hold `Y` while waiting for `X`, and that cycle cannot form.

writing.rule: Rust prevents data races, not deadlocks.

lessons.title: Pinning Intuition

answers: String implements Unpin, so this pinning wrapper does not forbid the move
Pin makes String thread safe
Pin gives the borrowed String a static lifetime
writing.exampleCaption: This complete safe program moves a String out through Pin because String implements Unpin. It contrasts with a location-sensitive !Unpin pointee.
writing.explanation:
`Pin` protects location-sensitive values after they are pinned; it does not make every value immovable from creation. Most users interact through pinned futures while libraries handle the `unsafe` construction details. Some future state machines can contain references into their own stored state while suspended. Moving such a value after those references become valid could invalidate them. `Pin

` is a contract that the value reached through pointer `P` will not be moved again if the value's type relies on pinning. It is not a magical freeze of every value from birth, and it does not mean the surrounding pointer variable can never move. Many ordinary types are `Unpin`, so pinning adds no movement restriction for them. A type that is `!Unpin` needs more care: once pinned, safe code must not move its inner value out through the pinned pointer. APIs that project pinned fields or construct self-referential structures carry subtle invariants. At this stage, use library-provided safe pinning helpers and avoid writing `unsafe` projections to make a compiler error disappear. Compare a plain `String`, which can be moved between bindings, with a future that a runtime stores and polls repeatedly. Think of pinning as protecting the address of the future's internal state across polls. Then read an API signature accepting `Pin<&mut F>` and identify what it promises to the future implementation. Do not infer that every `async` function creates self-references or that `Box::pin` is required for every future. The practical rule is to follow the executor and library API, and to treat `Pin` as a movement guarantee with a precisely defined start.
writing.feedback: Unpin opts a type out of pinning movement restrictions. The guarantee for an address-sensitive !Unpin pointee does not apply to this String.
writing.question: Why is moving the String out through Pin safe in this example?
writing.rule: `Pin` constrains moves of a pointee that relies on pinning. `Unpin` types such as `String` opt out of that restriction; moving the pointer wrapper itself is a separate matter.
writing.success: You can say why this safe move works for `String` and why it is unavailable for a `!Unpin` pointee.
writing.summary: Promise that a value will not move in memory.

lessons.title: Cancellation Safety

answers: Dropping that future; its body may not have started or may have suspended
Only reaching the end of the async body
Dropping any runtime join handle always cancels its task
writing.exampleCaption: One explicit poll saves state and then suspends. Dropping the future cancels the remaining acknowledgement, while saved=true remains observable.
writing.explanation:
Selecting or timing out a future may drop it before completion. Keep partial state consistent across `await` points, or wrap the operation so retrying cannot duplicate or lose external effects.

An owned future can be cancelled by dropping it before its first poll, before its body has run, or between polls after it has suspended. Work already completed before that point remains completed. A dropped future does not reverse a file write, database transaction, sent message, or charge to an external service. This creates a gap between “the caller did not receive a result” and “nothing happened.” Retry logic must account for that gap.

Consider `save_record().await` followed by `send_ack().await`. If the task stops between the two awaits, the record exists but the acknowledgement may not. Repeating the whole operation could create a duplicate record. Give each request a stable identifier and design the save as idempotent, or use a transaction/outbox pattern when the storage and notification must coordinate. Store enough progress that a restarted worker can decide what remains. A timeout tells the caller how long it waited, not whether the remote side performed the action.

Draw cancellation points on a three-step operation: prepare, commit, notify. At each point, list which externally visible effects already happened and what a retry would do. Test by injecting cancellation after the commit boundary. A guard can release an in-process mutex when dropped, but it cannot roll back arbitrary external effects. For spawned tasks, also check the runtime's ownership rules: dropping a handle may detach rather than cancel. Define both the cancellation path and the normal completion path before selecting a timeout or `select!` branch.
writing.feedback: A future can be dropped before its first poll or between polls. Dropping a task handle has separate runtime-specific semantics and may detach its task. Cancellation does not undo effects already performed.
writing.question: What cancels an ordinary owned future, including one that has not been polled?
writing.rule: Selecting or timing out a future may drop it before completion.
writing.success: You can point to where each flag is set and say why a retry must be idempotent after a drop.

lessons.title: Blocking in Async Code

answers: It stalls an executor worker
It moves the future
It poisons a lock
writing.exampleCaption: `.await` on a timer gives the thread back to the executor; `std::thread::sleep` would not.
writing.explanation:
A blocking call occupies an executor worker without yielding, so unrelated tasks can stall. Move CPU-heavy or blocking work to a dedicated pool and `await` its result.

An executor worker can poll many `async` tasks because each task yields while waiting for nonblocking I/O. A synchronous `sleep`, filesystem call, expensive compression loop, or blocking foreign-library call can occupy that worker instead. Other ready tasks then wait even though they could run. Putting `async` on a function signature does not change a blocking call inside it into cooperative work.

Use the runtime's blocking pool or a dedicated worker thread for truly blocking operations, and pass owned input into it. The offload has overhead, so a tiny calculation may be cheaper to perform directly; measure the latency of other tasks under realistic load. CPU-heavy jobs can saturate even a blocking pool, so consider a bounded queue or a separate compute service when throughput matters. Think about shutdown too: a blocking call may not stop simply because its `async` caller was cancelled.

Create one task that repeatedly awaits a short timer and logs the delay. Alongside it, run a second task with a long synchronous sleep. Observe the timer stalls when both compete for an executor worker, then move the blocking operation to the runtime's blocking facility and compare. Change the sleep to a CPU loop and watch the same scheduling issue. Keep track of where the result and error travel back to the `async` caller. The goal is predictable responsiveness, not merely making code compile inside an `async` block.
writing.feedback: There is no `.await` in that wait, so the task cannot yield. The worker is held for the full second, and other ready tasks on it wait too.
writing.question: Why is a blocking sleep harmful here?
writing.rule: A blocking call occupies an executor worker without yielding, so unrelated tasks can stall.
writing.success: The second task keeps its schedule, and you can say why `sleep` inside an `async fn` delayed it.
writing.summary: Keep executor threads available to poll other futures.
writing.task: Rewrite `handler` so the wait yields, using your runtime's async timer. Then run it beside a second task and compare how late that task's timer fires.

lessons.concept: Completion order, errors, and task lifetime

writing.summary: Keep the tasks you start in a collection whose lifetime and results are explicit.
writing.rule: Spawning starts an independent task; awaiting its result is a separate responsibility.
writing.explanation:
An async function creates a future, while spawning places that future under a runtime's scheduler. If your operation starts several child tasks, decide who owns their handles and who observes failures. JoinSet groups tasks returning the same type and yields their results in completion order. That order is not necessarily the order in which the tasks were inserted.

The example associates each result with its input index, drains the set with join_next, and sorts the collected pairs before presenting them. The sorting is a deliberate presentation policy, not an assumption about scheduler order. Handle the outer JoinError separately from any application Result returned inside a task: a task panic and a rejected input are different failures.

Dropping a JoinSet aborts its remaining tasks. This makes ownership visible, but abort is not a business-level rollback and does not undo effects already performed. A spawned blocking operation can have additional cancellation limitations. A reliable operation either drains its children, cancels them according to an explicit policy, or transfers their ownership to a longer-lived component.

For practice, make one child return an application error without panicking. Then make a different child panic and compare the two error layers. Do not require an exact completion sequence in the test; verify the set of indexed results. Keep real network work out of this exercise so scheduling behavior is not confused with a server or a backend execution service.

lessons.title: Bound Work Before Spawning
lessons.concept: Semaphore permits and bounded queues

writing.summary: Put the limit before the expensive resource allocation, not after an unbounded queue has formed.
writing.rule: A concurrency limit and a queue-size limit protect different resources.
writing.explanation:
A semaphore grants a finite number of permits. Holding a permit across the protected operation bounds the number of simultaneous operations. The important design question is where that permit is acquired. Spawning a million tasks that each wait for a permit still allocates a million waiting tasks; the semaphore has limited active work but has not bounded queued memory.

Acquire an owned permit before spawning each job when the producer should wait for capacity. Move the permit into the task and let it drop when that task finishes. This is backpressure: a fast producer cannot keep advancing independently of the consumer capacity. For a long-lived producer/consumer system, use a bounded channel as well, and decide whether a full queue waits, rejects, or drops according to the product's contract.

The example has six small jobs and two permits. It drains the JoinSet after submission and checks that every job completed. Because the runtime is current-thread, waiting for a permit yields so earlier jobs can run. Real I/O can overlap, but CPU-bound work does not become parallel here. A permit must cover the resource usage you intend to limit; releasing it before the expensive operation defeats that limit.

Test the policy using observable counters and an explicit barrier or yield, not timing guesses. Assert that the active count never exceeds the permit count and that every acquired permit is eventually returned after error paths. Do not use a zero-permit semaphore as a normal concurrency setting unless some other component will intentionally release capacity.

lessons.title: A Graceful Shutdown Protocol
lessons.concept: Stop admission, signal, and wait

writing.summary: Cancellation becomes reliable when the operation owns a protocol and a completion point.
writing.rule: Requesting shutdown is not the same as observing that all workers have stopped.
writing.explanation:
A useful shutdown sequence has three responsibilities: decide that shutdown is needed, notify the components that own work, and wait for their completion. Before signaling workers, stop accepting new work so the system cannot refill its queue forever. Then decide whether already accepted work is drained, rejected with an explicit result, or interrupted at a documented safe point.

The example uses a watch channel carrying a persistent boolean state. Each worker subscribes before the request and observes the current value before waiting for a change. That first check matters: a worker that starts after the value became true must not wait forever for another update. A watch channel represents the latest state, not a queue containing one shutdown message per worker.

After sending the request, the owner drains JoinSet and confirms that both workers acknowledged shutdown. This is deliberately an in-memory example without operating-system signals. A desktop service can translate ctrl-c into the same protocol, while a UI can translate an explicit Cancel action. The cancellation source and the worker contract remain separate so the protocol can be tested without terminating the process.

A real service also needs a deadline and escalation policy for stuck workers. Aborting a task is not a substitute for safe cancellation of a transaction or a blocking operation. Keep partial progress visible, release permits with RAII, and do not report that a save completed merely because the worker future was dropped. Test shutdown requested before subscription, during idle work, and after completion.

lessons.title: macro_rules!

answers: ident
expr
tt
writing.exampleCaption: Two arms, any number of arguments, all checked after expansion.
writing.explanation:
A declarative macro takes token trees, not values, so it can accept a variable number of arguments and shapes a function cannot. Fragment specifiers such as `expr` and `ident` say what each capture must be, and the expansion is type-checked afterwards like any other code.

A `macro_rules!` definition contains arms. Each arm has a pattern that matches input syntax and a transcriber that emits output syntax. The compiler tries arms in order. In `maximum!`, the one-expression arm ends recursion; the repeated arm captures one expression and a nonempty comma-separated rest. That is a compile-time transformation. Values are evaluated only when the expanded Rust code runs, and the expansion is type-checked in the caller's context. A macro can accept shapes that an ordinary function signature cannot, but this flexibility raises the cost of reading errors and maintaining the API.

Trace `maximum!(3, 9, 2)` on paper: the repeated arm reduces the tail, then compares the first expression with that result. Ask whether an argument with side effects is evaluated once. The temporaries `first` and `rest` keep each argument to one evaluation, and every arm deserves the same review. Use a function when types and arity are fixed; use a macro when syntax transformation or variable arity is essential. Keep exported macros small, document accepted forms, and test both successful expansions and expected compile failures. When an error appears far inside generated code, inspect the expansion and simplify the invocation until the mismatched pattern is clear.

Macro expansions can evaluate captured expressions more than once if the transcriber repeats them. For an expression with side effects, that changes program behavior. Use temporary bindings and inspect each arm. Also avoid returning a fragment with unexpected precedence; wrap a generated expression in a block or parentheses where its surrounding syntax could change how it is parsed.

lessons.title: Procedural Macros

answers: Only the serde crate as a normal dependency
A proc-macro crate compiled for and run on the host
Nothing special — derives are built into rustc
writing.exampleCaption: A separate crate, marked as a proc-macro, built for the host.
writing.explanation:
It receives a TokenStream and returns one, running as a real program during compilation — which is why it lives in its own crate compiled for the host machine. That host requirement is why a constrained device-local toolchain may not support arbitrary procedural macro crates; cross-compilation normally runs the macro on the build host.

A procedural macro is a Rust program that runs while another crate is being compiled. The compiler gives it tokens; it parses them, generates new tokens, and returns them to the caller's compilation. Derive, attribute, and function-like procedural macros differ in invocation shape, but all need a host-executable macro crate. The expansion is then checked as ordinary Rust code. This makes proc macros powerful for repetitive APIs and also makes their diagnostics, build time, and dependency chain part of the developer experience.

The host/target distinction matters for cross-compilation. A laptop may run the macro while producing code for a phone or WASM target. On-device compilation can support proc macros only if it can build or run compatible host artifacts and satisfy the required loading model; do not assume every constrained compiler can. Keep generated code independent of hidden target runtime state. In the example, the `Hello` derive should parse the input type, reject unsupported forms with a useful span, and emit an `impl` using stable paths. Try a trivial derive on a struct and then on an enum; make the unsupported form produce a clear compile error. Prefer a normal trait implementation when the implementation is short and explicit. Use generation when it removes repeated, mechanical code without hiding important behavior.

Generated code can fail to compile even when the macro itself runs successfully. Test the emitted implementation in a consumer crate and inspect the compiler errors there. A macro panic is poor feedback; report a structured compile error at the input span when possible. Avoid depending on the caller having a particular `use` statement unless the API explicitly documents it.
writing.feedback: serde_derive is a program the compiler runs, not just a library it links.
writing.question: What does that derive need at build time?
writing.rule: Proc macros execute at compile time, so they need a host-native build.
writing.success: You can name the host-compilation requirement as the reason.
writing.summary: A procedural macro is a compiler plugin written in Rust.
writing.task: Explain why a proc macro cannot run inside Crabrix.

lessons.title: cfg & Features

answers: Disable the dependency completely
Do not request its default feature set on this edge; other dependency edges can still enable it
Prohibit every feature throughout the entire dependency graph
writing.exampleCaption: Matching cfg predicates select the platform implementation; enabling extras adds a second print. Every branch retains valid Rust syntax.
writing.explanation:
`#[cfg(...)]` removes selected code before name and type checking, so platform-specific names need not resolve on other targets. Its source must still have valid Rust syntax. Cargo features are the same mechanism driven from the manifest, which is how one crate serves both a `no_std` embedded user and a full desktop one.

Conditional compilation decides which items exist in a particular build. A `#[cfg(target_os = "wasi")]` function is present only for matching targets; the opposite branch is present elsewhere. Cargo features are named inputs to this selection, often supplied by downstream users. Because a disabled branch is not part of the resulting item set, its behavior is not a runtime toggle and it must be checked in a build where it is enabled. Test the supported feature combinations rather than assuming the default build covers them.

Features in a dependency graph are generally additive: if two dependents enable different features of the same package, Cargo can compile that package with their union. Design features so enabling an extra capability does not silently remove another. For mutually exclusive choices, use explicit compile errors or separate types/configuration instead of pretending feature flags are exclusive switches. A `no_std` library might gate an allocation-backed helper behind a feature, but its core API must still compile without it. Run `cargo check --no-default-features` and a feature-enabled build for that design. Document what each feature changes, which target constraints it carries, and whether it affects public API. If callers need to choose at runtime, use a value or trait object instead of `cfg`.

Remember that code behind a disabled cfg may go untested for months. Put each supported target or feature combination into a build matrix that you can run locally or in release preparation. If a feature changes public types, document the resulting API surface for downstream crates. Do not use mutually exclusive features as a substitute for a real runtime configuration choice.
writing.feedback: Feature requests are unified for a package where Cargo resolves them together. This declaration omits defaults; it is not a graph-wide prohibition of std or of another named feature.
writing.practiceCode:
[features]
default = ["std"]
std = []

[dependencies]
memchr = { version = "2", default-features = false }
writing.question: What does default-features = false request on that memchr declaration?
writing.rule: `#[cfg(...)]` excludes selected code before name and type checking, but source syntax still has to parse. Disabling default features on one dependency edge does not prohibit another edge from enabling them.
writing.success: The other branch is absent from the build, not merely unused.
writing.summary: cfg decides which code is compiled at all.

lessons.title: unsafe Rust

answers: Nothing — unsafe makes any dereference legal
The pointer is non-null, aligned, and points at a live, initialised value
The pointer has to be declared mut before it is dereferenced
writing.exampleCaption: A small block, and the reason it is sound written next to it.
writing.explanation:
`unsafe` unlocks five powers. Inside an `unsafe` block you may dereference a raw pointer, call an `unsafe` function, access a mutable static, and read a union field; the fifth, implementing an `unsafe` trait, is an `unsafe impl` item, not something a block grants. Everything else is checked exactly as before. The block is a promise that you have verified an invariant the compiler cannot, which is why the convention is to write that invariant down as a SAFETY comment.

An `unsafe` block permits a small set of operations whose safety conditions cannot be fully checked by the compiler. It does not relax ordinary borrowing rules for safe references or make a wrong pointer valid. The lesson's `get_unchecked(0)` example is safe only because the slice is known to contain index zero at that exact call site. The `SAFETY` comment should connect the preceding check to the API's precondition. If a future edit changes that control flow, the proof must be reviewed again.

Prefer a safe operation when its cost is negligible or the optimizer can remove the check; `slice.first().copied()` is clearer here. Use `unsafe` only when a concrete boundary requires it, and make the boundary as small as possible. A safe wrapper around `unsafe` internals owes callers a sound contract for every input it accepts. Test edge cases such as empty slices, but remember tests cannot prove absence of undefined behavior. Audit aliasing, lifetimes, alignment, initialization, and thread interaction as applicable. Ask: what invariant is required, who establishes it, when can it stop holding, and can safe callers break it? That proof is the work behind the keyword, not an optional comment after the implementation.

A `SAFETY` comment should survive code review as an argument, not a ritual phrase. If the proof depends on a length check, keep that check close; if it depends on another module, link the invariant clearly. Revisit the comment whenever data ownership or concurrency changes. Reducing `unsafe` code to one audited helper often makes the rest of the program both faster to review and safer to extend. The test is whether safe callers can violate the claimed invariant.
writing.feedback: `unsafe` moves the obligation to you; it does not remove it.
writing.practiceCode: let value = unsafe { *pointer };
writing.question: What must be true for that to be sound?
writing.rule: `unsafe` is a claim about an invariant, not permission to skip the rules.
writing.success: No safe caller can trigger undefined behaviour.
writing.summary: `unsafe` unlocks five operations; it does not turn off the borrow checker.
writing.task: Wrap an unchecked operation in a safe API that cannot be misused.

lessons.title: FFI

answers: Nothing — Rust already matches the C layout
#[repr(C)] — Rust does not guarantee field order otherwise
The struct has to be declared pub for the C side
writing.exampleCaption: A declaration, a layout guarantee, and one `unsafe` call.
writing.explanation:
`extern "C"` selects the C calling convention and `#[repr(C)]` fixes field order so a struct matches its C counterpart. Unless a declaration is marked `safe fn`, every call is `unsafe`, because the compiler cannot see the other side, and ownership must be agreed explicitly — who allocates, who frees, and how long a borrowed pointer stays valid.

An FFI boundary is a contract shared by two languages. The ABI determines how arguments and return values cross the call; `#[repr(C)]` helps a Rust struct follow C field order and padding rules for the target. It does not make every Rust type valid for C: `String`, `Vec`, and Rust enums without an explicit representation need a deliberate interface. Prefer fixed-width integer types where the C declaration requires them and check the target's definitions for `size_t`, pointers, and alignment.

In the example, `abs` takes and returns a C `int`; the Rust declaration must match the actual C header on that target. For a pointer argument, document whether the callee may write, retain the pointer, or free it. If Rust owns a buffer, keep it alive for the whole call and do not let C retain it unless the API explicitly transfers ownership. Translate C error codes or null pointers into `Result` or `Option` in a small safe wrapper. Compile a tiny cross-language test against the real library, including boundary values. Do not rely on the Rust compiler to detect a signature mismatch it cannot see. The best FFI module exposes an ordinary safe Rust API while keeping the foreign assumptions visible and auditable in one place.

Also consider callbacks crossing back into Rust. The C library may call them later, from another thread, or after shutdown. A Rust closure cannot be passed as a bare function pointer without a deliberate trampoline and context lifetime. Keep callback ownership and thread assumptions in the same contract as pointer validity. A working happy-path call proves little about those edges.

In Rust 2024, foreign declarations use `unsafe extern "C"` blocks; that spelling is also accepted in earlier editions. Calling a foreign function remains unsafe unless its declaration explicitly establishes otherwise. These examples require a matching linked foreign implementation and illustrate a desktop ABI boundary, not support for arbitrary native C libraries in Crabrix. For C `abs`, the minimum signed integer is not a valid argument when its positive magnitude cannot be represented; the fixed -42 example avoids that boundary.

`#[repr(C)]` on an outer struct does not change the representation of an inner field’s type. Define C-compatible representations for nested by-value data too. The resulting size, padding and alignment still depend on the target ABI; do not use an in-memory C layout as a portable file or network format. Document allocator pairing, pointer length and validity, nullability, callback lifetime and unwinding separately.
writing.feedback: Without `repr(C)` the layout is unspecified and the C side may read the wrong bytes. Rust's `improper_ctypes` lint warns about this declaration.
writing.practiceCode:
struct Point { x: f64, y: f64 }

unsafe extern "C" { fn distance(p: Point) -> f64; }
writing.question: What is missing from that struct?
writing.rule: `repr(C)` follows C layout rules for the target; it is not a recursive layout, ownership or pointer-validity guarantee.
writing.success: The ownership contract is written down, not assumed.
writing.summary: FFI needs explicit ABI, layout, ownership and validity contracts; unsafe code must uphold the foreign function requirements.
writing.task: Declare a foreign function and describe who owns any memory it returns.

lessons.title: Performance

answers: Take &[String] and drop the clone
Return a reference to the first name
Use a HashMap
writing.exampleCaption: One allocation up front instead of a handful of geometric regrowths.
writing.explanation:
`Iterator` chains can optimize similarly to hand-written loops, but inspect representative hot paths rather than assuming identical machine code. What does cost is allocating in a hot loop, cloning to satisfy the borrow checker, and choosing the wrong container. Reserve capacity when the size is known, borrow instead of cloning, and measure with the profile and target you intend to ship. Debug timings describe that debug build; they are not a reliable prediction of optimized performance.

Performance work begins with a workload and a measurement. A release build is essential because debug checks and missing optimizations can dominate a microbenchmark. Use realistic input sizes and record latency distributions or throughput, not one attractive timing. Profile before changing code: time may be in parsing, allocation, I/O, locking, or an algorithmic choice far from the line that looks complicated. An iterator chain is often optimized well, but verify hot paths rather than treating any syntax as inherently free or expensive.

In the example, `Vec::with_capacity(1_000)` avoids repeated growth when the final size is known. It does not avoid initializing each pushed element. Borrowing a slice in `total` avoids cloning the vector just to read it. Next, compare a linear search with a `HashMap` lookup for your actual access pattern; the map's build cost and memory overhead can outweigh faster repeated lookups for a tiny input. Change one variable at a time, rerun under similar conditions, and keep a correctness test alongside the benchmark. State the tradeoff: perhaps more memory buys lower tail latency, or an extra allocation simplifies a cold path. Optimize the measured bottleneck and stop when the improvement is no longer meaningful to the product.

Beware of a fast path that worsens the slowest cases. Reserving capacity may reduce allocations but increase peak memory if most inputs are tiny. A hash map may speed lookup while making iteration order unsuitable for a UI. State the workload distribution and the user-visible metric before choosing the optimization. Keep the simpler version if the measured gain is negligible.
writing.feedback: The clone is never needed: map already produces new Strings.
writing.question: Which change removes the wasted work?
writing.rule: Measure representative workloads with the target optimization profile; debug timings do not predict release performance.
writing.success: Behaviour is unchanged and the allocation count drops.
writing.summary: Rust is fast by default; the wins left are allocation and algorithm.
writing.task: Find one clone or one allocation in a loop and remove it.

Distinct types make a wrong argument order a compile error

writing.exampleCaption: Two integers that can no longer be confused for each other.
writing.explanation:
A newtype gives a bare value a meaning the type system can enforce, so a UserId cannot be passed where an OrderId belongs. A builder makes many optional parameters readable, and typestate encodes a protocol in types so calling a method in the wrong order simply does not compile.

Rust idioms use types and ownership to make intentions visible. A `UserId` newtype prevents accidentally passing an `OrderId`, even though both wrap `u64`. It is a zero-cost distinction in ordinary compiled code, but you still need explicit conversion at serialization and database boundaries. `Option` expresses absence; `Result` expresses failure with context. These enums make callers handle states that might otherwise be hidden in nulls or sentinel integers. Use pattern matching when it makes the state transition easier to read.

A builder is valuable when an object has several optional settings or validation before construction. Typestate goes further by representing stages as different types, so only a configured value exposes `send()`. Both patterns add API surface and can be overkill for a small internal helper. Start with a simple constructor; add richer types when misuse is likely or the workflow truly has stages. In the example, attempt `load_user(OrderId(7))` and use the compiler error to explain the boundary. Then design a `ParsedConfig` that can become `ValidatedConfig` only after checking required fields. The goal is to encode stable domain rules, not to make every local variable into a wrapper. A good idiom reduces the amount of explanation needed at each call site.

Watch for type complexity that merely moves confusion. A builder with dozens of states can make an API harder to discover than a validated configuration struct. Show users a normal construction path in documentation, and keep error messages close to invalid input. Types are strongest when the domain invariant is stable and the compiler can give a clear failure at the call site.

writing.question: What does a newtype fix here?
writing.rule: A newtype costs nothing at runtime and buys a real compile-time guarantee.
writing.success: Mixing it with another id of the same underlying type fails to compile.
writing.summary: Rust's patterns push mistakes from runtime to compile time.

lessons.title: Macro Hygiene

answers: The defining crate
The caller variable
Cargo.lock
writing.exampleCaption: `$crate::value` keeps pointing at the defining crate wherever the macro is expanded.
writing.explanation:
Rust macros track syntax context so identifiers introduced by a macro do not casually collide with names at the call site. Use explicit paths such as $crate for helper items exported with a macro.

A macro can introduce identifiers in the caller's scope, and those names must resolve predictably. Rust's syntax contexts protect many identifiers introduced by a declarative macro from accidentally capturing a similarly named local value. This is hygiene, but it is not a reason to ignore names entirely: exported macros still need a stable way to refer to helper items from their defining crate. `$crate::helper` points to that crate even when a caller renames its dependency. A plain unqualified helper name may accidentally resolve in the caller's scope or fail there.

Try exporting a macro that calls an internal helper and invoke it from a separate crate. First use an unqualified helper name and observe the failure. Then use `$crate::helper` and ensure the helper is reachable in the way the expansion needs. If the macro creates a local temporary, choose a small scope and test with a caller variable of the same spelling. Also test the macro when the dependency is renamed in `Cargo.toml`. Inspect expanded code when a diagnostic seems to point at an unfamiliar name. Hygiene reduces accidental capture, while explicit paths and careful API tests make an exported macro dependable across crate boundaries.

When a macro is exported, run a small downstream consumer test rather than invoking it only inside its defining crate. The consumer catches path assumptions that local tests hide. Give public helper items namespaced paths and avoid relying on imports that happen to be present in one caller. This keeps the macro usable as the crate evolves.

lessons.title: Token Trees

answers: A Rust expression
Any text
A type only
writing.exampleCaption: `:expr` captures a whole expression, and the `let` evaluates it once before it is used twice.
writing.explanation:
`macro_rules!` consumes token trees with balanced delimiters. Fragment specifiers such as `expr` and `ty` let the parser validate shapes before expansion, producing safer patterns than string substitution.

Rust tokenizes macro input into structured pieces. Identifiers, punctuation, and literals are tokens; balanced parentheses, brackets, and braces form delimited groups that can contain more tokens. A macro does not receive raw characters to split by hand. In a function-like invocation such as `show!({a, b})`, the name `show` selects the macro, while the input stream inside the invocation contains a brace group with `a`, a comma, and `b`. Keeping that boundary clear prevents confusion when reading a procedural macro parser.

A `macro_rules!` pattern can ask the compiler to parse a fragment as an expression, type, identifier, or other supported shape. A pattern like `($value:expr)` rejects input that is not an expression before the transcriber runs. Repetition syntax can accept comma-separated lists, but test empty input, a single item, and a trailing comma explicitly. For the example, expand `twice!(2 + 3)` by hand and notice that the temporary evaluates the expression once before adding it to itself. That matters if the expression has side effects. Treat macros as syntax APIs: define accepted forms, produce readable errors, and avoid making a clever pattern harder to understand than an ordinary function.

Delimiter groups matter for error reporting too: a missing closing brace changes the token tree before your macro matcher sees it. Distinguish lexical or parse errors from a pattern that simply did not match. Keep an example for every arm in documentation, especially if one arm accepts an optional comma or nested group; syntax APIs deserve the same testing care as functions.

writing.rule: `macro_rules!` consumes token trees with balanced delimiters.

answers: On the build host
Inside the target app
In Cargo.toml
writing.exampleCaption: The function runs in the compiler's host process, and the tokens it returns join the crate being built.
writing.explanation:
A procedural macro is compiled for and runs on the build host, then emits tokens for the target crate. It cannot depend on target runtime state and should emit spans that point errors back to useful input.

Procedural macros run as host tools during compilation. They receive token input from the crate being built and return token output that the compiler later checks for the target. If you cross-compile from a Mac to a phone, the macro runs on the Mac; generated program code targets the phone. This is why host dependencies and target dependencies can have different requirements, and why a restricted on-device compiler may not support arbitrary proc-macro crates. Keep the generated program independent of accidental host-only paths or environment details.

Good diagnostics are part of the macro's public API. A derive that rejects an unsupported enum should point to the enum or offending field rather than failing with a cryptic token-stream panic. Parse input using an appropriate syntax library when available, preserve useful spans, and add compile-fail examples for invalid forms. Avoid doing network or filesystem work at expansion time unless the build contract explicitly depends on it; such hidden inputs make builds difficult to reproduce. Test the macro in a separate consumer crate, including renamed dependencies and generic types. If a small trait implementation is clearer without generation, prefer it. A proc macro should remove mechanical repetition while making the generated contract easier, not harder, to audit.

A procedural macro is code executed during the build, so dependency updates to that crate deserve the same review as other build tooling. Pin versions where reproducibility matters and avoid hidden environment-dependent output. If the macro emits code with an unexpected import, prefer absolute paths or documented helper crates. The generated API should still be understandable without reading the macro implementation.
writing.feedback: `host_os!` runs on the build host during compilation and pastes its answer into the target program as a string literal.
writing.question: Where does a proc macro execute?
writing.rule: A procedural macro is compiled for and runs on the build host, then emits tokens for the target crate.
writing.success: You can say which value belongs to the build host and which to the target.

lessons.title: Raw Pointers

answers: Dereferencing
Creating the pointer
Printing the value
writing.exampleCaption: Creating the pointer from `&value` is safe; the `unsafe` block covers only the read, while `value` is alive.
writing.explanation:
Creating `*const T` or `*mut T` is safe; dereferencing one is `unsafe` because validity, alignment, initialization, and aliasing are now the programmer's proof obligations.

A raw pointer such as `*const T` or `*mut T` can represent a location without the safety guarantees that a normal Rust reference carries. Constructing one from a valid reference is safe. Dereferencing it requires `unsafe` because the compiler cannot prove that the pointed-to object is still alive, aligned, initialized, in bounds, and accessed under valid aliasing rules. A raw pointer may carry provenance information about its allocation; treating it as merely a numeric address can miss part of the memory model.

In the example, `pointer` is created from `&value`, and `value` remains alive while the pointer is read. That local reasoning supports the `unsafe` dereference. Change the example conceptually so the pointer outlives `value`; now the proof fails even if the numeric address still looks plausible. Never use a runtime test as proof that dereferencing an invalid pointer is safe: undefined behavior may appear to work once. Keep the `unsafe` operation close to the checks that justify it, and expose a safe API only when callers cannot violate those assumptions. For FFI, additionally document who owns the allocation and when the foreign side may retain or free the pointer.

Pointer arithmetic adds more obligations: an offset must stay within the permitted allocation rules even if it is not dereferenced immediately. Do not infer validity from a non-null address alone. Prefer slices, references, and `NonNull`-based library APIs when they express the invariant safely; a raw pointer is useful at FFI and data-structure internals, where its proof can be tightly contained.
writing.feedback: Creating and printing the pointer are safe, since neither touches the memory behind it. Only the dereference needs `unsafe`, and here its proof fails.
writing.question: Which operation needs `unsafe`?
writing.rule: Creating `*const T` or `*mut T` is safe; dereferencing one is `unsafe` because validity, alignment, initialization, and aliasing are now the programmer's proof obligations.
writing.success: You can name the proof the example has and this snippet lacks: `value` is still alive when the pointer is read.

lessons.title: Representation & Layout

answers: To define its layout
To allocate it on the heap
To make it Copy
writing.exampleCaption: `repr(C)` keeps `kind` first and aligns `length` to its own boundary, with padding between them.
writing.explanation:
Rust's default layout may change for optimization and is not an FFI contract. `repr(C)` gives C-compatible field ordering while fixed integer types make sizes explicit.

Rust's default struct representation is chosen for Rust code, not as an external wire or ABI contract. `#[repr(C)]` requests C-compatible field ordering and layout rules for the target, including padding between fields. It does not make a struct packed, remove padding, or guarantee the same total size on every architecture. Fixed-width fields such as `u16` and `u32` make individual sizes explicit, but alignment and endianness still matter when bytes cross a file or network boundary.

For the example `Header`, draw offsets for `kind` and `length` under a typical C layout and locate any padding before the `u32`. Then compare the result with a C declaration built for the same target. Use `size_of` and `align_of` as checks, not as the only specification. Do not serialize a `repr(C)` struct by copying its raw bytes into a protocol: padding can be uninitialized, and a different machine may use another byte order. Define a wire format with explicit field widths and endianness instead. Reserve `repr(C)` for genuine language or ABI interoperability where both sides agree on ownership and representation.

For unions, bitfields, and packed data, the boundary becomes more complicated than a simple struct. A packed field may be unaligned, so taking an ordinary reference to it can be invalid. Read or write such representations through the appropriate unaligned operations when required. Most application data should use a deliberate parser rather than treating external bytes as an in-memory Rust struct.
writing.feedback: `repr(C)` fixes field order and padding, so on a typical target `length` sits at offset 4, after two padding bytes.
writing.question: Why does an FFI struct need `repr(C)`?
writing.rule: Rust's default layout may change for optimization and is not an FFI contract.
writing.success: You can locate the two padding bytes and say why the default layout is not an FFI contract.

lessons.title: Unsafe Traits

answers: Callers rely on its promise
Traits are never checked
Its struct holds an array
writing.exampleCaption: A narrow contract makes the implementor's proof concrete: zero is a valid `u8` and therefore a valid Byte.
writing.explanation:
An `unsafe` trait means incorrect implementation can cause undefined behavior in code that trusts it. Document every invariant precisely and keep the `unsafe impl` beside evidence that it holds.

An `unsafe` trait is a promise whose incorrect implementation can invalidate assumptions made by other code. Its documentation must state the invariant precisely: which operations, lifetimes, alignment, or thread interactions are safe, and what every implementor must maintain. The `unsafe` keyword on the `impl` means the implementor has checked that contract; it is not a compiler proof. A generic caller may rely on the trait bound and therefore cannot recheck each concrete implementation.

Avoid vague contracts such as “instances never expose moves” unless the type truly enforces that property. A plain `FixedBuffer` can be moved between bindings, so claiming stable address for it would be unsound. For a learning example, use a narrow contract instead, as `ZeroIsValid` does: the all-zero bit pattern must be a valid value of the type. The standard `Send` is another precise contract: a type may be transferred to another thread only when doing so cannot cause a data race or invalid access. Examine every field before adding an `unsafe impl`; a non-atomic shared pointer can break that claim. Prefer safe auto traits and existing library abstractions wherever possible. If you must author an `unsafe` trait, write a safety section with concrete counterexamples, place each `impl` beside its proof, and review changes to the type's internals against that proof.

The teaching trait example has no consumer that relies on the promise, so it illustrates syntax rather than proving a real `unsafe` abstraction. In production, state exactly what `unsafe` generic code may assume from the bound. Then try to construct a counterexample type and see whether the proposed contract rules it out. If the contract cannot be written precisely, the trait is not ready to publish.
writing.feedback: Unsafe code may rely on the trait's promise without rechecking it. The keyword marks the implementor's claim, and the compiler accepts it even though this one is false.
writing.question: Why must that `StableAddress` impl be written `unsafe`?
writing.rule: An `unsafe` trait means incorrect implementation can cause undefined behavior in code that trusts it.
writing.success: You can say why `ZeroIsValid` for `Byte` holds and why `StableAddress` for `FixedBuffer` is unsound.
writing.summary: Make an implementation promise other `unsafe` code relies on.

lessons.title: Benchmark & Profile

answers: Measure a workload
Rewrite the hot loop from intuition
Raise opt-level blindly
writing.exampleCaption: `Instant` times one run of `workload`, and `black_box` discourages the compiler from removing it.
writing.explanation:
A benchmark measures a stable workload; a profiler explains where its time or allocations go. Change one variable, protect against optimized-away work, and compare distributions rather than one lucky run.

A benchmark asks how a specific workload behaves under controlled conditions. A profiler asks where time, allocations, or waits occur during that workload. Start with a question that matters to a user, such as median parse latency for a typical file or worst-case response time for a large project. Use a release build, warm up when appropriate, and keep input, hardware, and environment stable between comparisons. One `Instant` measurement is useful for a quick observation but too noisy to settle a small optimization.

A compiler may remove work whose result is unused, so a benchmark must keep the result observable; `black_box` can help prevent an obvious optimization in a microbenchmark but does not make the benchmark realistic by itself. Record a distribution over repeated runs and look for variance from caching, scheduling, and I/O. Profile the slow case before changing code. If allocations dominate, reserve capacity or borrow data; if the algorithm scales poorly, a container or complexity change may matter more. Change one variable, rerun the same workload, and keep a correctness test. Report both the improvement and its cost in memory, code complexity, or startup time.

For a before-and-after report, include the input shape, sample count, median and slower-tail observations, build mode, and what you held constant. If the result is within the noise, say so. A useful profile names the expensive path and gives enough context to reproduce it; a colorful flame graph without a workload description is not an engineering conclusion.
writing.feedback: A measured workload tells you what is slow and gives a number to compare after a change. A rewrite from intuition or a higher `opt-level` without one is a guess.
writing.question: What should happen before optimization?
writing.rule: A benchmark measures a stable workload; a profiler explains where its time or allocations go.
writing.success: You can report sample count, median, and build mode, and say whether the change beats the noise.
writing.summary: Find the real bottleneck before optimizing.
writing.task: Run this in a debug and a release build and compare the medians. Then change `iter().sum()` to a version you think is faster, and report both numbers.

writing.summary: A WebAssembly module runs with the imports its host supplies, not with every capability of the computer.
writing.rule: Compilation target and host imports determine what a module can do.
writing.explanation:
Rust is the source language; WebAssembly is an execution format; WASI is a family of host interfaces. They are separate layers. A module targeting wasm32-unknown-unknown does not automatically get a filesystem, sockets, or the browser DOM. A wasm32-wasip1 program expects the corresponding WASI imports, which a browser does not provide merely by supporting WebAssembly.

Crabrix supplies a local runtime and its supported host interfaces. In the browser, a worker and runtime adapter can compile or execute locally while the website serves toolchain assets. Downloading a compiler is network activity, but it is different from sending source to a backend compiler. Shared documents can use a relay without granting another participant the right to execute source on your device.

A browser DOM integration needs a JavaScript boundary or another deliberate adapter. A guest filesystem is likewise a host-provided view; its paths are not unrestricted paths on the phone. If a library assumes operating-system processes, native threads, or unsupported networking imports, having Rust source alone does not make it compatible with this target.

Local compiler profile for this lesson's small exercise: standard-library text inspection only. The exercise classifies import names according to an explicitly supplied allowlist; it does not inspect a real module or implement a security policy. Real runtime validation must parse the binary, check actual imports and limits, and preserve the host's sandbox. Keep educational models distinct from the enforcement used by a production engine.

lessons.title: Linear Memory Boundaries
lessons.concept: Checked offsets, lengths, and borrowed slices

writing.summary: A guest pointer is an offset into guest memory, not a host pointer you can blindly dereference.
writing.rule: Check offset plus length without overflow before making a borrowed view.
writing.explanation:
A host function receiving a guest pointer and length must interpret them relative to that module's current linear memory. First validate the requested range, then borrow only the verified bytes. An offset is not a native pointer, and a numerically small address does not establish permission. A length can overflow when added to the offset even if each input separately fits its integer type.

The lab models this boundary with a Rust byte slice and usize offsets. Use checked_add for the end offset and slice::get for the bounds check. Return None for overflow or an out-of-range end. An empty range at memory.len is valid, while an empty range beginning after memory.len is invalid. This precise convention avoids special-case pointer arithmetic that accidentally accepts an invalid start.

Decoding text is a second check. A valid byte range can contain invalid UTF-8, so use from_utf8 if the interface requires text. Do not reinterpret arbitrary guest bytes as a Rust struct whose alignment, layout, or validity requirements may not hold. Copy or decode a documented wire representation instead.

Local compiler profile: standard library only. The model uses no unsafe code and does not implement a runtime memory manager. In a real embedding, memory growth and reentrant calls may invalidate a cached host view, so follow the runtime's borrowing rules and reacquire the view at the appropriate boundary. Tests of this pure function do not establish that a separate native runtime binding follows those rules.
writing.exampleCaption: Checked offsets, lengths, and borrowed slices
writing.task: Borrow the requested byte range or return None. Check addition overflow. A zero-length range at the end is valid; a start past the end is not. In the Crabrix app, open the compiler lab and complete the supplied function in solution.rs. The reading question is a separate exercise.

writing.question: Is an in-bounds byte slice necessarily valid UTF-8?
answers: No; text decoding requires another validation step
Yes, because all memory is UTF-8
Only if its length is even

writing.summary: Local execution still needs independent limits for the resources a guest can consume.
writing.rule: A timeout does not replace memory, output, or filesystem quotas.
writing.explanation:
A local playground executes untrusted source on the user's own device, so a useful sandbox must bound more than filesystem access. A program can loop forever, allocate aggressively, print without end, or fill its writable directory. Each consumes a different resource. A wall-clock deadline alone may detect a slow run only after memory or output has already exhausted the host.

Define budgets at the layer that owns the resource. An interpreter may provide fuel or interruption for instruction execution; the host can cap captured output and writable bytes; the embedding can limit memory pages and concurrent runs. Cancellation should release the owned run and its resources, while the UI reports a quota stop distinctly from a successful program exit or an ordinary Rust diagnostic.

The compiler lab is a small model of output accounting. Starting from a known usage, accept the next chunk only if checked addition stays within an inclusive limit. Refuse overflow and an already-invalid starting state. An empty chunk at the exact limit is valid. This function does not enforce the actual runtime's limits; it teaches why checking after an unbounded allocation is too late.

Local compiler profile: standard library only. In a shared Playground, code and selection changes may be interactive while execution remains local and explicit. Another participant's Run should update shared output metadata rather than start your device's compiler. A production safety review must test those event boundaries separately from this arithmetic model, including disconnection, repeated messages, and a local cancel during remote edits.
writing.exampleCaption: Independent CPU, memory, output, and storage limits
writing.task: Return updated usage only when checked addition succeeds and the inclusive limit is respected. Reject an invalid starting usage as well as overflow. In the Crabrix app, open the compiler lab and complete the supplied function in solution.rs. The reading question is a separate exercise.
writing.success: The local compiler accepts the changed solution and the separate verification harness finishes all normal and boundary cases. Printing a success message alone does not complete this lab.
writing.question: Which statement about a local execution timeout is correct?
answers: It makes all allocations safe before it fires
It automatically limits printed output to one line
It is one limit and does not replace separate resource quotas
writing.feedback: CPU time, memory, output, storage, and concurrency need limits at their own boundaries.
